59ec699e9f:c5a3d1516354aed9.title: The Supply-Side Effect of Immigration on Prices: Evidence from Nursing Homes
59ec699e9f:c5a3d1516354aed9.author: Izabela Wnuk-Soares
59ec699e9f:c5a3d1516354aed9.summary: We study how immigration affects prices through changes in labor supply. Using policy-driven increases in immigration to Germany and administrative data covering the universe of nursing homes, we find that one additional foreign-born woman per 100 residents reduces nursing-home care prices by 2.6 percent. The price effects are concentrated in more competitive markets. Examining potential mechanisms, we find that immigration lowers labor costs as nursing homes shift toward lower-paid foreign-born workers. We find no evidence of declines in inspection-based measures of quality or of scale effects. Finally, immigration increases the use of informal care, potentially strengthening competitive pressure from the broader care market.

59ec699e9f:1c8d3748e52f0cc5.title: AI-Augmented Capital-Skill Complementarity
59ec699e9f:1c8d3748e52f0cc5.author: Roberto Pinheiro
59ec699e9f:1c8d3748e52f0cc5.summary: We model artificial intelligence (AI) as a distinct capital input in a nested CES aggregate production function that extends work done by Krusell et al. (2000) and embed it in a dynamic general equilibrium economy. By bringing the model to the data, we estimate the degree to which AI either substitutes for or complements the other production inputs at the aggregate level. We find that AI is complementary to the high-skill–equipment composite and that the AI weight in production remains small. We then use the model to study how this complementarity shapes the macroeconomic and distributional effects of AI capital accumulation. The estimated model implies different effects of alternative AI shocks. A rise in the AI usage share is contractionary as it increases reliance on a scarce complementary input. A fall in AI prices is expansionary due to the lower cost of accumulating AI capital. A tax on AI capital income raises limited revenue while the AI capital stock remains small, but can finance welfare-improving transfers as the AI price falls. A large-scale universal basic income (UBI) funded jointly by a consumption tax slows AI investment with welfare gains for low-skill workers at the expense of losses for high-skill workers and entrepreneurs. On the measurement side, we construct a quality-adjusted AI price index from hedonic regressions and build a corresponding AI capital stock.

59ec699e9f:1f9e3fda07812288.title: Crime, Spatial Reallocation, and Employment Dynamics: Evidence on Firm-Size Heterogeneity from Mexico City
59ec699e9f:1f9e3fda07812288.author: Monserrat Zuñiga Loreto
59ec699e9f:1f9e3fda07812288.summary: This paper examines the relationship between neighborhood crime and firm employment in Mexico City. Using a balanced panel of 2, 354 Basic Geostatistical Areas (AGEBs) for 2017--2022, we estimate Spatial Durbin Models with AGEB fixed effects, lagged and winsorized crime variables, and differential trends by dominant firm-size stratum, decomposing total effects into direct and indirect components. At the aggregate level, robberies are negatively associated with employment in the AGEBs where they occur, alongside positive spillovers toward neighboring areas. This aggregate pattern conceals substantial heterogeneity: large firms (101 or more employees) are the only stratum with a negative and significant direct effect, whereas small firms (0--10 employees) show a positive direct effect, consistent with structural immobility and the local reallocation of displaced demand. Medium-sized firms show negative but imprecisely estimated effects. A dynamic specification preserves these signs but is weakly identified once persistence is absorbed. Crime appears to reallocate employment across the firm-size distribution and across space rather than uniformly contracting local labor demand.

59ec699e9f:30a9651e21805b4f.title: The Long-Term Effects of Labor Market Restrictions on Women’s Cognitive Aging
59ec699e9f:30a9651e21805b4f.author: Dorly Deegdijk
59ec699e9f:30a9651e21805b4f.summary: This study examines the causal effect of labor market restrictions faced by women in early adulthood on later-life cognitive functioning. To identify this effect, we exploit an exogenous policy change in the Netherlands that removed restrictions on married women's access to paid employment in 1957. Our study draws on data from the Longitudinal Aging Study Amsterdam, an ongoing cohort study of older individuals. We focus on individuals aged 75 and older born between 1928 and 1947. We first examine how work restrictions in early adulthood shape lifetime employment. Next, we assess how these work restrictions affect women’s later-life cognitive outcomes exploiting an exogenous change in labor restriction laws and complement this with an instrumental variables approach. The estimation results indicate that restricted access to paid employment for women in early adulthood reduced labor force participation and occupational prestige over the life course. These reduced labor market opportunities, in turn, led to poorer cognitive functioning after age 75. We also find some suggestive evidence that these restrictions resulted in faster cognitive decline. Taken together, our findings indicate that restrictions on women’s access to paid employment adversely affect cognitive functioning, thereby contributing to cognitive disparities between men and women in later life. More broadly, they highlight the long-term cognitive benefits of sustained labor market engagement and cognitively stimulating work, with potential implications for dementia prevention.

59ec699e9f:3bf831fa255a51f9.title: Matching and Mentoring: Effects of Managers on Worker Productivity
59ec699e9f:3bf831fa255a51f9.author: Chengyuan Hua
59ec699e9f:3bf831fa255a51f9.summary: This paper studies how managers matter for worker productivity by exploiting manager moves in Major League Baseball. I first show that manager effects are primarily match-specific using an AKM-type model. Then, staggered difference-in-differences results show positive effects of shared characteristics, including same position, both lefties, and same hometown. Effects of same position and both lefties are larger than same hometown. Effects are more pronounced for younger and less productive workers, indicating that mentoring is the primary mechanism while in-group bias is secondary. Finally, there is suggestive evidence that a managerâ€™s productivity as a worker is not a positive characteristic.

59ec699e9f:5f08d505bc269652.title: World War I and Female Labor Force Participation: The Case of England and Wales
59ec699e9f:5f08d505bc269652.author: Milner, Benjamin
59ec699e9f:5f08d505bc269652.summary: Combining district-level measures of World War I military fatalities with full-count census microdata, we show that wartime mortality increased postwar female labor force participation in England and Wales. Women shifted away from traditionally female occupations, while military deaths increased the shares of single and widowed women, whose participation rates were higher. Yet the overall effect of military mor-tality on postwar female labor force participation remained modest. A harmonized comparison with France suggests that stronger internal migration in England and Wales rapidly dissipated local marriage- and labor-market imbalances, while more generous pensions for war widows weakened their labor supply response.

59ec699e9f:c9bac5dd6367f0dd.title: Beyond the Paycheck: Using Fringe Benefits to Attract a Broader Pool of Applicants
59ec699e9f:c9bac5dd6367f0dd.author: Thea S. Zoellner
59ec699e9f:c9bac5dd6367f0dd.summary: Many firms in tight labor markets recruit for highly gender-segregated occupations, leaving them, in effect, drawing from only half the potential labor pool. We study how firms can use fringe benefits to attract workers and influence occupational choice. Unlike occupation-specific recruiting strategies, fringe benefits can be added to any occupation; they are also easily tailored, implemented, and scaled. Using a personalized and incentivized discrete choice experiment, we present participants with job options that match their skills and work task preferences. Within each option, we vary salary, occupation, and fringe benefits that adolescents had classified as gender-neutral, male-typed, or female-typed. We find that fringe benefits are highly valued: their effect is around a third as large as having prior interest in the occupation. Neutral and stereotypical benefits in particular improve perceptions of the firm across multiple dimensions. Furthermore, we find substantial gender differences. Female-typed benefits deter male participants, whereas all other benefit-participant combinations have a positive effect. Female participants value benefits more when those benefits are paired with an atypical occupation, and we find suggestive evidence that this reflects benefits alleviating concerns about limited support in such roles. In addition, male-typed benefits can increase the attractiveness of gender-atypical occupations for female participants. Female participants who consider atypical occupations place relatively higher value on these benefits and tend to exhibit less traditionally feminine preferences. We also find suggestive evidence that anticipated social reactions, particularly from parents, accompany these choices.

59ec699e9f:2934120f38330147.title: Religion Versus Religiosity: What Matters for Hiring?
59ec699e9f:2934120f38330147.author: Baert, Stijn
59ec699e9f:2934120f38330147.summary: Religious discrimination in hiring is rarely studied independently from ethnic discrimination. We fill this gap using a preregistered factorial survey experiment in which professional recruiters evaluate candidate profiles that independently vary by ethnic majority versus minority names, visual religious signals, and volunteering activities signalling either Christian or Muslim religious affiliation. Beyond hiring intentions, we measure recruitersâ€™, colleaguesâ€™, and customersâ€™ anticipated willingness to work with candidates, as well as recruitersâ€™ HEXACO personality assessments of the candidates. Candidates whose religious position recruiters identify receive lower interview ratings than candidates whose position remains unclear to them, and this penalty does not differ between Christian, Muslim, and atheist attributions; interview propensity declines further as attributed religiosity rises; and among the assigned signals, only religious volunteering reduces hiring chances. Religious candidates are not regarded as less diligent or less honest, but as less likely to be accepted by others.

59ec699e9f:06c77b4b9eef9aab.title: GLP-1 Treatment and Work Capacity
59ec699e9f:06c77b4b9eef9aab.author: Sergio Galletta
59ec699e9f:06c77b4b9eef9aab.summary: Using linked Finnish administrative records and a staggered difference-in-differences design, we estimate how starting semaglutide (Ozempic) affects work capacity, measured by medically certified sickness absence. The first purchase is followed by persistent use and improved glycemic control, indicating that recorded purchases correspond to sustained and clinically active treatment. The reduction in sickness absence is near zero during months 0–5, becomes progressively larger thereafter, and is largest during months 12–18. Averaged over event months 0–18, sickness allowance receipt falls by 16.9 percent and compensated days by 14.3 percent relative to pre-treatment means. The decline in full-day sickness absence is not offset by greater reliance on unemployment or partial sickness benefits. The results show that semaglutide improves work capacity and can generate economic benefits beyond its direct effects on metabolic health.

59ec699e9f:e1d0a860f381ab05.title: How to Increase the Mental Well-Being of Your Employees? An Overview of Research Testing Interventions in the Workplace
59ec699e9f:e1d0a860f381ab05.author: Baert, Stijn
59ec699e9f:e1d0a860f381ab05.summary: This systematic literature review provides a state-of-the-art overview of the effectiveness of workplace interventions aimed at improving workersâ€™ mental well-being. Specifically, it examines which types of interventions are effective for which aspects of mental well-being, both in the short and long term. To this end, we identify 125 randomised controlled trials comprising 147 interventions that vary in their objectives (prevention, treatment, or reintegration), targets (workers or work), methods (cognitive, meditation-based, physical, ergonomic, organisational, or multimethod) and delivery channels (offline, online or hybrid). Mental well-being outcomes are classified as biological and self-reported indicators of the three components of subjective mental well-being (evaluative, affective, and eudaimonic well-being). Overall, we find that, for preventing and treating early mental health symptoms, cognitive or meditation-based interventions targeting personal coping resources appear most promising. In contrast, successful reintegration seems to require a combination of cognitive and organisational interventions, with the latter addressing job demands and resources.

59ec699e9f:1d01c428371127e6.title: A competitive world
59ec699e9f:1d01c428371127e6.author: Tungodden, Bertil
59ec699e9f:1d01c428371127e6.summary: We provide globally representative evidence on two attitudes toward competition: individuals’ willingness to compete and the importance they attach to boys and girls being willing to compete, using a novel survey module that we fielded as part of the 2022 Gallup World Poll. The data cover more than 66, 000 individuals across 62 countries. Men are more willing to compete than women in all but two countries, and willingness to compete is higher among younger, more educated, and higher-income individuals. Attitudes toward children’s willingness to compete vary substantially across countries, with competitiveness valued more for boys in some countries and for girls in others. Both attitudes are systematically related to the economic and social environment. Individuals exposed to greater inequality or faster population growth during their formative years are more willing to compete and place greater importance on children being willing to compete. Greater exposure to gender equality during formative years is associated with smaller gender gaps in both adults’ willingness to compete and attitudes toward the competitiveness of boys and girls. Our findings reveal striking global regularities while highlighting the role of the social environment in shaping attitudes toward competition.

59ec699e9f:2cf24bcb7e8bda5a.title: Labor share, FDI and Productivity
59ec699e9f:2cf24bcb7e8bda5a.author: Krekó, Judit
59ec699e9f:2cf24bcb7e8bda5a.summary: This paper examines how foreign direct investment affects the labor share through productivity differences between foreign- and domestically owned firms. We develop a search-and-matching model in which more productive foreign firms acquire domestic firms. Foreign ownership raises productivity and wages, but incomplete pass-through of the productivity advantage to workers reduces the labor share. Using European industry-level data, we find that greater foreign employment penetration is associated with lower labor shares and that the foreign productivity premium substantially exceeds the foreign wage premium. Hungarian administrative firm data show the same pattern: foreign-owned firms have higher productivity and labor costs but lower labor shares. Event-study estimates around foreign acquisitions are less precise but are consistent with this mechanism at longer horizons. Our results show how economies with a large foreign-owned sector can combine relatively high wages with relatively low labor shares and highlight persistent foreign–domestic productivity differences as a potential explanation for labor-share differences across Europe.

59ec699e9f:349e7186d4483924.title: Carbon Taxation, Firm Performance, and Labor Demand
59ec699e9f:349e7186d4483924.author: Karlsson, Jimmy
59ec699e9f:349e7186d4483924.summary: Carbon taxation is one of the main policy instruments for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, yet there is still limited evidence on its effects on firms and workers. This paper studies the environmental and economic effects of carbon taxation, with a particular focus on heterogeneity in labor demand across worker groups. I exploit a reform that increased the effective carbon tax for a subset of Swedish manufacturing firms between 2011 and 2018, and combine administrative firm data with matched employer-employee records in a difference-in-differences design. The reform reduced emissions by about 30%, primarily through substitution away from fossil fuels toward biofuels and district heating. It also reduced revenue and employment, with the strongest negative effects concentrated among emission-intensive firms. The employment effects are driven mainly by older workers without a high school degree, although older, highly educated workers are also negatively affected in the most exposed firms. Additional evidence suggests that firms adjusted labor demand primarily through lower hiring rather than higher separations. Scaled by the average increase in effective tax rates (measured in euro per ton CO2), the estimates imply semi-elasticities of -0.58% for emissions and -0.20% for employment among low-educated workers. These results suggest that carbon taxation can substantially reduce industrial emissions, but with concentrated labor-market costs.

59ec699e9f:f8ae0c16a535be81.title: Permanent residency policy and skilled immigration: Evidence from a Swedish reform
59ec699e9f:f8ae0c16a535be81.author: Lundberg, Erik
59ec699e9f:f8ae0c16a535be81.summary: Aging populations and labor shortages in skill-intensive sectors have led many countries to pursue targeted policies to attract international talent. We study a migration reform in Sweden that offered international doctoral students from outside the EU an easier path to permanent residency. Implemented in 2014, the reform shortened the required period of residence from eight to four years, allowed these students to obtain permanent residency immediately after graduation, and granted their spouses a work permit during their doctoral studies. Using the European students as a comparison group in a difference-in-differences design, we find that the treated international students are 10.5 pp (18%) more likely to stay in Sweden three years after graduation. Higher settlement prospects also increase their language investments and marriage rates during the PhD. These effects are larger for cohorts that have longer exposure to the reform and for those who carry out their doctoral research in STEM. In addition, the reform raises both employment and language investments among the partners of the treated international students. Taken together, the policy increases permanent residency among international graduates as well as leads them and their families to make long-term choices conducive to integration. Finally, using a shift-share design, where we combine the reform with the pre-existing variation in the share of international students across research fields, we find positive peer effects on residency. More international students settling in Sweden increases the probability of their European peers making the same choice.

59ec699e9f:605aeb37cee5fef9.title: Beyond the Unemployment Rate: A Structural Labor Market Indicator
59ec699e9f:605aeb37cee5fef9.author: Damjan Pfajfar
59ec699e9f:605aeb37cee5fef9.summary: Labor market variables frequently send conflicting signals about the degree of slack or tightness, often complicating policy assessments at critical junctures. This paper develops a Structural Labor Market Indicator (SLMI) for the U.S. economy that addresses the limitations of existing univariate measures or atheoretical statistical approaches that synthesize multiple labor market indicators but cannot distinguish between supply and demand driving forces. We construct the SLMI using a medium scale New Keynesian DSGE model featuring search and matching frictions, endogenous labor force participation, and variable hours. The model is disciplined by a comprehensive dataset that includes not only labor market variables but also other macroeconomic aggregates. The SLMI synthesizes model-implied gaps across multiple labor market dimensions using principal component analysis. We show that GDP growth and inflation provide substantial information about labor market slack beyond what labor market variables contain, validating our multi-variable structural approach. Relative to alternative measures, the SLMI often provides earlier warnings of deteriorating conditions at recession onset but recovers more gradually during expansions.

59ec699e9f:bab2c540887d0eca.title: Spatial mobility and the risk of dropping out of vocational education and training in Germany: Costs, resources, and returns
59ec699e9f:bab2c540887d0eca.author: Wicht, Alexandra
59ec699e9f:bab2c540887d0eca.summary: Vocational education and training (VET) dropout disrupts school-to-work transitions. While spatial mobility is an important strategy for accessing VET, little is known about how it relates to subsequent dropout. Drawing on a cost-benefit perspective, this study examines whether first-year VET dropout differs by spatial mobility and whether these differences vary with resources available to bear mobility-related costs and returns that may offset them. We use representative longitudinal data from the German National Educational Panel Study linked to administrative geospatial data. Logistic regression models distinguish non-mobile students from those mobile within and between regional labor markets (RLMs) and assess heterogeneity by parental socioeconomic status (SES), VET wages, realized occupational aspirations, regional attractiveness, and regional person-environment match. Predicted dropout probabilities are approximately three percentage points higher for mobility within RLMs and four points higher for mobility between RLMs than for no mobility. These mobility-related differences decrease with increasing parental SES for both mobility types. Higher VET wages correspond to smaller dropout differences for mobility within RLMs, whereas greater realization of occupational aspirations corresponds to smaller differences for mobility between RLMs. Higher regional attractiveness shows a similar pattern only for mobility within RLMs, while higher regional person-environment match coincides with smaller dropout differences for both mobility types. Overall, mobility-related dropout differences vary with available resources and realized returns. The social patterning of mobility-related dropout differences may contribute to inequalities in school-to-work transitions, underscoring the importance of considering spatial mobility and regional contexts in research on youths’ educational decision-making.

59ec699e9f:ec357d3932d02e7b.title: When Is the Mover-Design Event Study Coefficient a Place-Effect Share?
59ec699e9f:ec357d3932d02e7b.author: Vahid Moghani
59ec699e9f:ec357d3932d02e7b.summary: Mover-design event studies are a leading approach to separating place effects from sorting. The coefficient is often interpreted as the share of cross-sectional variation in location means due to places. I show the coefficient depends on how movers connect locations: two economies can be identical in place effects, sorting, and location means, yet deliver different mover coefficients. Only under directional isotropy, a testable condition, does the coefficient permit a cross-sectional reading: it averages the variance share of place effects and the share that equalizing them removes. An illustration in Dutch employerâ€“employee wage data rejects the condition.

59ec699e9f:0381cb4524899e6a.title: The Cost of Women's Labor Supply and Occupational Choice Frictions
59ec699e9f:0381cb4524899e6a.author: Arato, Hiroki
59ec699e9f:0381cb4524899e6a.summary: This paper quantifies women's occupational choice frictions between manufacturing and services in Japan from the early 2000s to the late 2010s using a general equilibrium Roy model. We then decompose changes in women's sectoral employment propensities relative to men's into comparative-advantage and friction components. In the full sample (ages 20–59), the model-implied occupational distortion moves closer to the frictionless benchmark, whereas in the young subsample (ages 20–34), it shifts from manufacturing-biased to service-biased by the late 2010s. Over the same period, women's comparative disadvantage in manufacturing narrows, especially in the young subsample. Within the model, changes in comparative advantage and occupational choice frictions largely offset each other, so women's sectoral employment propensities relative to men's change only modestly. Counterfactual simulations show that output losses from occupational choice frictions evolve differently across the two samples: they decline sharply in the full sample but increase in the young subsample. Specifically, the output loss falls from about 18% to about 4% in the full sample, whereas it rises from about 6% to about 10% in the young subsample.

59ec699e9f:12b1fbb9671761bc.title: Intangible Capital, Markups, and Markdowns: Evidence from Japanese Listed Firms
59ec699e9f:12b1fbb9671761bc.author: YAMAMOTO, Yohei
59ec699e9f:12b1fbb9671761bc.summary: This paper examines how intangible capital is related to firms' market power in product and labor markets using an unbalanced panel of Japanese listed firms from 1980 to 2024. We estimate firm-level markups and markdowns following the production-function approaches employed by the standard literature and then relate these measures to two types of intangible capital: R&D stock and organizational capital. The empirical results show that organizational capital is positively associated with markups and negatively associated with markdowns, while the role of R&D stock is relatively limited and less robust. These findings suggest that organizational capital may strengthen firms' product-market position while also encouraging rent sharing with workers. The stagnant accumulation of organizational capital may therefore help explain why Japan experienced weak price and wage growth since the 2000s.

4a32a2255e:c915fbf11c3ceae5.title: The Geography of Life Chances and Intergenerational Mobility
4a32a2255e:c915fbf11c3ceae5.author: Connor, Dylan Shane
4a32a2255e:c915fbf11c3ceae5.summary: We have entered a new era of soaring inequalities in income and wealth, patterns driven by a highly differentiated landscape of opportunity. This economic reality has propelled the geographies of intergenerational mobility and life chances to the forefront of the social science agenda. While geographers are increasingly engaging with these topics, the field of economic geography provides a critical, yet underutilized, theoretical foundation for this work. This chapter proposes the People-Experience-Places (PEP) framework, a model for analyzing the geographic differentiation of life chances across space and time. Drawing from core schools of thought within economic geography, the framework identifies the foundational mechanisms that produce spatially differentiated opportunity regimes and their impact on intergenerational mobility. The chapter concludes with a call for economic geographers to return to the core concerns of understanding and addressing inequalities in livelihood possibilities.

4a32a2255e:581561d3d3520369.title: The Geographic and Sectoral Impact of Productivity
4a32a2255e:581561d3d3520369.author: Del Valle Fuentes, Miguel Angel
4a32a2255e:581561d3d3520369.summary: To understand the geographic and sectoral impact of productivity, we build the first input-output matrix disaggregated at the geographic level within a country using unique administrative data harmonized to match national accounts. We use this data from Chile to calibrate a state-of-the-art general equilibrium quantitative trade model with production networks, labor mobility, firm selection, international and domestic trade, congestion of fixed factors, and knowledge diffusion. We consider two applications. First, we study the aggregate effects of local productivity shocks. We show that location-sector interactions are crucial: locations and sectors separately account for less than half of the dispersion in GDP elasticities from location-sector- specific productivity shocks. Geography-specific input-output linkages explain 16% of the dispersion, due to the role played by small and influential markets. Second, we analyze the exit of a large steel plant. We show that geographically disaggregated production linkages substantially increase the propagation of the plant exit.

4a32a2255e:f12807b3380a05fe.title: Estimating Regional Industry Employment from Economic Location Mechanisms: A Constrained Spatial Disaggregation for European Geographies
4a32a2255e:f12807b3380a05fe.author: Boero, Riccardo
4a32a2255e:f12807b3380a05fe.summary: Fine-scale employment by industry is largely unavailable across European municipalities, yet it underpins regional economic analysis, environmental-economic extensions, and the regionalization of input--output accounts. This paper presents a mechanism-driven, constrained spatial disaggregation framework that estimates industry employment down to the Local Administrative Unit level while preserving official totals exactly at every geographical level. The economic mechanisms that shape where activity locates --- settlement, infrastructure and accessibility, natural-resource endowments, and inter-industry co-location --- are represented as a reproducible input dataset assembled from official and remote-sensing sources; a family of constrained allocation models, combined by a cross-validated convex ensemble, is trained on data-rich United States geographies and transferred to Europe under official Eurostat totals as constraints. Validated against independent national statistics in Italy, France, Germany, and Spain, the estimates reproduce the observed spatial distribution of employment within the held-out uncertainty of the models themselves, and the error does not inflate down the four-step disaggregation. The framework is open, inspectable, and reproducible, providing internally consistent fine-scale employment estimates wherever sub-national industry data are sparse.

4a32a2255e:9fed8a98586b464a.title: Agglomeration and Fragility: Firm Responses to the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake
4a32a2255e:9fed8a98586b464a.author: Eric Strobl
4a32a2255e:9fed8a98586b464a.summary: In this paper we investigate how the disruption of local agglomeration economies affects firm adjustment following a catastrophic urban disaster. To this end we digitalized a unique survey of firms in Tokyo City completed shortly after the earthquake and before any government reconstruction intervention. Using detailed information on the damage experienced by firms and the main good that they produced, as well as where they were located, we construct measures of losses of local agglomeration economies by identifying firms that either permanently ceased operation or relocated elsewhere. To identify causal impacts we exploit plausibly exogenous variation in fire destruction generated by the interaction between fire outbreak locations and local wind direction and speed immediately after the earthquake. Our econometrics results show that a loss of agglomeration economies as a result of the earthquake had a substantial impact on firms shutting down or relocating, with average effects of 13 and 11 per cent for these outcomes, respectively.

4a32a2255e:ea5b5b61b8ec50ed.title: When London Burned to Sticks: The Economic Impact of the Great Fire of 1666
4a32a2255e:ea5b5b61b8ec50ed.author: Tsoukli, Xanthi
4a32a2255e:ea5b5b61b8ec50ed.summary: This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the Great Fireâ€™s effects on Londonâ€™s economic geography. Our analysis reveals both continuity and change. There was a swift postfire recovery accompanied by some shift in economic activity towards the City of Westminster by 1690, with markets spreading outside the City, but financial services largely remaining inside. Analysis of London Hearth Tax records further illustrates a significant change in the wealth distribution, with wealthier households returning to fire-impacted areas, reshaping the cityâ€™s housing and social structure.

33e1d7779a:d97879045963f423.title: AI panic sparks rare bipartisan moment on Capitol Hill
33e1d7779a:d97879045963f423.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:d97879045963f423.summary: Lawmakers who want to regulate AI are doing something unusual as Congress barrels towards a lengthy recess with no tangible solution in sight: They're working across the aisle. Why it matters: Bipartisanship is increasingly elusive on Capitol Hill of late, but it remains a crucial first step for action in a Senate that requires 60 votes to pass most legislation. The latest example: Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) are pressing congressional leadership for a vote on their bill to establish a federal program to assess and monitor AI systems. "Recent incidents of rogue AI agent swarms hacking into public websites and systems have removed lingering doubts concerning the ability of these agents to wreak havoc on our cyber infrastructure," the pair wrote in a letter first obtained by Axios. "Congress cannot delay legislating to address frontier AI risks much longer. Industry-led evaluations are not enough." State of play: Several new bipartisan efforts to regulate AI have cropped up in the week since several current and former employees at Anthropic and OpenAI went public with concerns about the existential risks posed by their own products. Reps. Russell Fry (R-S.C.) and Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) are founding a caucus focused on AI small businesses, called the Innovators Caucus, as Axios first reported Monday. Among the group's stated goals is starting work on a federal framework to regulate AI, as well as bringing small businesses to the AI policymaking table. The doomsday warnings have also breathed new life into existing bipartisan proposals to mitigate the dangers of AI. Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) has been publicly hawking his bill with Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) to require AI companies to include a human-activated "kill switch" in their systems. Lieu has also privately pitched Democratic leadership on creating a bipartisan AI select committee if they retake control of the House next year. Reps. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) and Jay Obernolte…

33e1d7779a:924e2bb08fb3511d.title: House GOP's Epstein files headache is back
33e1d7779a:924e2bb08fb3511d.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:924e2bb08fb3511d.summary: The Epstein files fight that consumed the House last year is threatening to engulf Republicans all over again. Why it matters: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) is now just one Republican away from having the support he needs to force another politically painful Epstein vote — and he and his allies are hunting for the final GOP signature. Retiring Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) signed Massie's new discharge petition Monday, joining Massie and Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.). Massie and Mace told Axios they're actively targeting retiring Republicans and members in vulnerable districts for the fourth GOP signature that will get them the magic number to force a vote on the Epstein Files Transparency Act II. Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), one of four Republicans who bucked President Trump and GOP leadership to sign Massie's first Epstein petition last year, told Axios she's considering signing again and has been having conversations with Massie. The big picture: The push is reviving one of the most disruptive fights of Trump's second term for House Republicans. Last year's Epstein discharge petition became a months-long headache for Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and the White House before ultimately securing 218 signatures and forcing the issue onto the House floor. The bill passed with almost unanimous support in the House. The Epstein Files Transparency Act II would enforce and expand the release of remaining files at DOJ. "The Department of Justice continues to unlawfully withhold over 3 million Epstein files that should be released to the public. In addition, the DOJ is unlawfully maintaining heavy redactions on the files it is releasing," Massie wrote in a s tatement last month . Reality check: Even if Massie locks down the Republican support he needs this week, the House is set to leave Washington Thursday until after the November midterms, meaning any potential floor showdown would come post-election. Democrats also still need to provide the remaining signatures needed to reach…

33e1d7779a:58f465c242ebaf0b.title: How Ed Sheeran's tour imploded over a geopolitical fight
33e1d7779a:58f465c242ebaf0b.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:58f465c242ebaf0b.summary: Ed Sheeran's world tour spiraled into chaos this week after one opener was removed, every remaining opening act quit and stadiums threatened to pull the plug on the tour. Why it matters: The turmoil reveals the power dynamics behind major concert tours, showing how even a global star like Sheeran can be forced to take a back seat on decisions about his own shows. Driving the news: All four of Sheeran's remaining supporting acts announced Tuesday that they were dropping out. Irish musicians Aaron Rowe and Beoga , as well as Danish band Lukas Graham , said Tuesday they were leaving the tour. Rowe was set to replace Macklemore as the opener for the U.S. shows, AP reports. Finneas, who was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year, also announced he was exiting the concert series, saying on Instagram that "artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed." Catch up quick: The moves came one day after rapper Macklemore, who was scheduled for most of the remaining tour dates, was dropped after using his sets to voice support for Palestinians and condemn the war in Gaza during shows on Sept. 4-5 at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. Macklemore told the MetLife crowd on Sept. 4 that he wanted to do the tour so he could "say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine.'" His performance included images of war-torn Gaza playing on the video board. The tour's promoters, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone Monday that concert venues threatened to cancel shows unless Macklemore was dropped from the tour after his pro-Palestinian comments. Zoom in: Macklemore said the decision came after he spoke with Sheeran, alleging that the headliner faced pressure from stadium owners including Robert Kraft, owner of the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium. According to Macklemore, Sheeran is typically "apolitical" and the recent round of backlash "challenged" him "in a way it never had before." The other side: Sheeran shared…

33e1d7779a:33c41e5ebe09157a.title: House quashes another Trump impeachment push with Dem help
33e1d7779a:33c41e5ebe09157a.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:33c41e5ebe09157a.summary: The House voted for the third time in two years to quash a rogue effort by Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) to impeach President Trump. Why it matters: As with the last two times, the vote divided House Democrats. Some sided with Green, but others voted "present" or actively helped GOP leadership defeat the effort. Green frustrated his Democratic colleagues by forcing the vote without support from party leadership, with one telling Axios the move was "fucked up." The Texas Democrat defended his attempts to impeach Trump over killings committed by federal immigration officials, calling it a "life and death" matter. Driving the news: The House voted 232-147 for Republican leadership's measure to table — effectively, kill — Green's motion to force a vote on impeaching Trump, with 47 members voting "present." Between the lines: Some Democrats who voted with Green privately sneered before the vote that it was a distraction from party messaging on the House's last in-session week before the midterm. Green pushed back by saying the lawmakers who criticized him "don't have the courage to stand up and face me" and challenging them to debate the matter publicly.

33e1d7779a:203cabe0ec4e2624.title: Trump-aligned Kennedy Center board votes to close building
33e1d7779a:203cabe0ec4e2624.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:203cabe0ec4e2624.summary: The Kennedy Center's board voted Tuesday to close the iconic performing arts center's main building for a renovation project championed by President Trump , multiple outlets reported and a source familiar confirmed to Axios. Why it matters: Trump's attempts to put his name on the building , which memorializes former President John F. Kennedy, have fueled an ongoing legal and political battle. The decision came hours after a federal judge again said the center could not put Trump's name on the building . Driving the news: Axios could not immediately confirm when the closure will happen or how long it will be. A resolution from the board, filed as evidence in the ongoing legal fight with Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) over the Center, listed ways Trump could be "legally and appropriately recognized" on the building, after a federal judge ruled that only Congress can change its name. The resolution cited "water intrusion and deterioration of the center's physical plant" that it said "caused a partial ceiling collapse," arguing the safety risk "greatly outweighs any reputational risk associated with closing the main building." Zoom out: A second resolution filed on Monday listed ways Trump could be "legally and appropriately recognized" on the building, after a federal judge ruled that only Congress can change its name. The resolution states that without his name on the building, it's "unlikely" Trump "will provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building." It listed options for text on the exterior marble beneath the center's name, including "A Legacy protected through the Generosity of President Donald J. Trump" or "Renovation, Restoration, and support by President Donald J. Trump." Friction point: U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper blocked the center from closing earlier this year, finding that "the Board was derelict in discharging the full range of its responsibilities to the Center" and "based its decision on an insufficient, one-sided…

33e1d7779a:75b68fe3d9121b02.title: Scoop: Trump pollster gives GOP a data center survival guide
33e1d7779a:75b68fe3d9121b02.author: Alex Isenstadt
33e1d7779a:75b68fe3d9121b02.summary: President Trump's longtime pollster is offering Republican candidates a detailed playbook for neutralizing Democratic attacks over AI data centers — down to what language they should and shouldn't use. Why it matters: Republican strategists say GOP candidates have been all over the map in responding to the backlash to data centers. The goal is to put Republicans on offense after months of playing defense on the issue. Driving the news: Pollster Tony Fabrizio warns in a two-page memo obtained by Axios that "unqualified support for building more AI data centers is a losing position." Fabrizio specifically advises candidates not to say, "I support building more data centers," warning: "It will be clipped and show up in ads." Instead, he tells Republicans to support AI infrastructure only if developers pay for their own power needs, protect consumers from higher utility bills and safeguard local water and natural resources. Fabrizio argues that candidates must make clear those conditions are enforceable, rather than voluntary commitments from tech companies. "This converts the candidate from a defender of technology companies into the person imposing rules on them," Fabrizio writes in the memo, which was sent Monday. Fabrizio offers a three-step script for candidates. First, "validate" voters' concerns about higher utility bills, the power grid and water use. Second, "draw the line" by vowing not to support projects that force families to subsidize them or allow tech companies to harm surrounding communities. Finally, argue that projects should move forward only if companies provide their own power, protect ratepayers and safeguard local water. "The order matters," Fabrizio writes. "It adopts voters' concerns as the approval standard instead of asking them to set those concerns aside." Fabrizio warns against generic support for "more data centers," leading with jobs or China, dismissing local concerns or defending individual projects before their costs and resource…

33e1d7779a:07ceef7f54def9b4.title: Trump considered dangerous, corrupt by majority in new poll
33e1d7779a:07ceef7f54def9b4.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:07ceef7f54def9b4.summary: Data: The Economist/YouGov ; Chart: Avery Lotz A slight majority of registered voters describe President Trump as corrupt and dangerous, a recent poll found, while just 14% say he isn't divisive. The big picture: Simply put, polling hasn't been pretty for the president — or for his Iran war , tariffs or other top priorities . Still, with the midterms weeks away, Trump has centered himself, making the election a referendum on his presidency . By the numbers: " Corrupt" (53%) and "dangerous" (51%) led the list of descriptors voters applied to Trump in the Sept. 11-14 The Economist-YouGov poll of 1,461 U.S. registered voters. Those words were followed by "out-of-touch" (47%), "cruel" (46%) and "bold" (45%). Just 18% said they'd use the word "steady" to describe the president. Worth noting: Democrats are testing an anti-corruption midterm message as Americans' perceptions of government corruption hit a 20-year high , per Gallup's trend , and polls show Americans believe the president has inappropriately profited from cryptocurrency while in office. The results broke sharply by party — 91% of Democrats and 62% of independents said Trump was corrupt, compared with 10% of Republicans. Republicans weren't universally positive: Less than half (49%) said they'd use the word "honest" to describe the president. Just 10% said it didn't describe him, while 41% had no opinion. Similarly, 38% of Republicans said he was steady, while 53% said they had no opinion. What they're saying: White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in an emailed statement that "President Trump has launched an all-out war on fraud across the entire federal government, holding criminals accountable and saving taxpayers billions of dollars." Ingle also accused Democrats in Congress of failing to stop waste, fraud and abuse in government. Zoom out: Trump's approval rating ticked up from the lowest point of his political career, recorded last month in Reuters-Ipsos' trend , this month. Some 35% of Americans…

33e1d7779a:8937b2505ec704e8.title: Massie moves to impeach Pete Hegseth over Iran War
33e1d7779a:8937b2505ec704e8.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:8937b2505ec704e8.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced a resolution Tuesday to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , accusing him of defying Congress and illegally continuing the U.S. war in Iran. Why it matters: The impeachment effort is a long shot in the GOP-controlled Congress, but Massie's resolution is privileged, meaning he can force a full House vote and put Republicans on the record over Hegseth's handling of the Iran war. It's a dramatic escalation in the retiring lawmaker's months-long push to rein in the Trump administration's war powers. The effort also comes after the House has repeatedly voted on efforts to constrain the administration's military campaign in Iran, including passing war powers resolutions in June and July directing the president to end U.S. hostilities with Tehran. The House is slated to vote Tuesday on another war powers resolution on the Iran war effort. Driving the news: Massie's resolution accuses Hegseth of carrying out orders to continue operations in Iran despite Congress' constitutional authority over war and its votes seeking to end the conflict. Massie argued Hegseth's actions "frustrated Congress's ability to exercise its most solemn constitutional responsibility" and allowed an "unlawful war" to continue. "In all of this, Secretary Hegseth has acted in a manner contrary to his trust as Secretary of Defense," Massie said on the House floor. The eight-article resolution also targets Hegseth over U.S. military operations in Venezuela and Yemen, including accusing him of illegally directing the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization. Zoom out: Hegseth already faced a separate impeachment push from House Democrats, who introduced six articles against him in April that included allegations he waged an unauthorized war against Iran. What's next: The House will have to take up the legislation within the next two legislative days, but GOP leaders could also move to vote on tabling the…

33e1d7779a:3edb7a6d47983688.title: Kennedy Center's attempt to put Trump's name on building blocked again by judge
33e1d7779a:3edb7a6d47983688.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:3edb7a6d47983688.summary: A federal judge ruled Tuesday that the Kennedy Center's latest attempt to put President Trump's name on the performing arts center violated his earlier order blocking its renaming . The big picture: The order came just before the Kennedy Center's board, now composed of Trump loyalists, is set to weigh shutting down the building for renovations that members argue must include Trump being "appropriately recognized" on the structure. Driving the news: While Trump allies have argued the latest attempt to recognize Trump does not violate the law, U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper said "[l]inguistic gymnastics cannot extricate the Kennedy Center's Board from an operative judicial order or the governing statute it was designed to enforce." Cooper ordered for Trump's name to be removed from the building in May, saying only Congress could change the name of the center that memorializes President John F. Kennedy. The judge blocked the center from putting an inscription that read "renovated and restored by Donald J. Trump" on the main building or renaming the campus the "President Donald J. Trump Plaza." Cooper wrote, "Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing." This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:331d4536f995c29f.title: Trump turns on the Supreme Court he helped build
33e1d7779a:331d4536f995c29f.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:331d4536f995c29f.summary: President Trump lashed out at the Supreme Court on Tuesday after it struck down the president's mail-in voting order Monday night. Why it matters: The president slammed the justices over rulings they've issued against him this year, suggesting without evidence that the three justices he appointed to the court are being controlled by the left. What they're saying: "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "[T]hey are merely a shell of their original selves, a Court that is costing the United States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings that are of such magnitude that it won't be easily possible for our Country to recover or heal. "It is a Court that will go down as having rendered some of the most destructive, hurtful, and damaging decisions in our Country's history." "It is not easy for me to write this criticism of the United States Supreme Court - it will likely cost me dearly for years to come - but I feel it my obligation and duty, as President, to do so for the America we love!" Zoom in: Trump unloaded on the court for striking down his birthright citizenship policy, in which the justices upheld that those born on American soil are citizens. He also slammed their "horrible decision on Tariffs ," after they ruled those unlawful earlier this year. "Certain Justices are petrified of these crazed and depraved Democrats, and are totally unable to show the courage necessary to save our America," Trump wrote. Between the lines: Without naming them, Trump criticized the three justices he appointed: Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. He explicitly praised Justices Alito and Thomas, who dissented in Monday's mail-in ballot ruling. The Supreme Court could not be immediately reached for comment. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:eaa87cd3584cdb32.title: Scoop: U.S. attacked Iranian boats trying to seize Navy drone
33e1d7779a:eaa87cd3584cdb32.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:eaa87cd3584cdb32.summary: The U.S. military destroyed two Iranian small boats Monday after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps tried to steal a Navy drone patrolling the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. officials told Axios. Why it matters: The unusual incident shows how efforts to restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz continues direct confrontation with Iran . The U.S. military initially didn't disclose the strike, and Iranian media presented it as a drone strike on "fishing boats." Driving the news: According to Iranian media , two fishing boats were struck Monday off the coast of the port city of Kargan and near Larak Island in Hormozgan province. Ahmad Nafisi, the province's deputy governor for security affairs, attributed the strike to the U.S. military. Nafisi said an unspecified number of fishermen were missing and that search-and-rescue operations were underway, according to Iran's semi-official Mehr News Agency. Behind the scenes: A U.S. official said the IRGC used the boats to try to capture a naval drone that the U.S. military uses to patrol the Strait of Hormuz. After U.S. forces identified the attempt, an American drone fired two missiles at the boats, destroying them and killing most of those on board. What they are saying: U.S. Central Command spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins confirmed the attempted seizure, saying "Iranian small boats recently attempted to take possession of a U.S. unmanned surface vessel, but they were unsuccessful after CENTCOM forcefully responded." "The surface drone remains under U.S. operational control," Hawkins said. State of play: The incident took place as the U.S. attempts to protect increased commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, where oil flows remain below prewar levels. A U.S. official said the U.S. military and Gulf countries have begun conducting daytime transits of tankers through the strait and not only night time as was the case in recent month. As fighting with the Houthis in the Red Sea escalates, Saudi Arabia has…

33e1d7779a:5011ce21f4a8cd57.title: House Democrats face divisions on Russian sanctions bill
33e1d7779a:5011ce21f4a8cd57.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:5011ce21f4a8cd57.summary: House Democratic leadership is vocally opposing a Russia sanctions bill set to come to a vote this week, but not all of their members are comfortable taking that stance just yet. Why it matters: Republicans will reportedly need some Democratic votes to make up for defections from their isolationist wing and pass the measure. At issue for many Democrats is that the bill, named in honor of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), would allow the Trump administration to impose up to 100% tariffs on the five top importers of Russian oil. That has forced Democrats to choose between two issues that have become shibboleths for their party: support for Ukraine and opposition to giving President Trump more power to set trade policy. State of play: Reps. Greg Meeks (D-N.Y.), Don Beyer (D-Va.) and Richard Neal (D-Mass.) — the ranking members of the House Foreign Affairs, Joint Economic and Ways & Means committees, respectively — announced their opposition to the bill in a joint statement last week. "House Democrats are rock solid in our support for Ukraine, but the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia And Iran Act would do more harm than good," they said. "This bill would dramatically expand presidential tariff authorities while failing to mandate sanctions on Russia, both of which are unacceptable." Yes, but: Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine), an arch-centrist who often breaks with party leadership, told Axios last week he is "almost certainly going to be a 'yes' on the bill. "I think the sanctions [are good] but I am also generally supportive of tariffs," said Golden. The Maine Democrat has been his party's lone cheerleader for many of Trump's more controversial protectionist trade measures. Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) , the co-chair of the bipartisan Congressional Ukraine Caucus, told Axios she is "reviewing [the bill] very carefully" and "working with our Ukraine Caucus." "I think it's important to send Russia a message that she needs to stand down," Kaptur added. Rep. Mike…

33e1d7779a:be7129a6dc7b6f71.title: Scoop: Top House Democrat launches investigation into Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding
33e1d7779a:be7129a6dc7b6f71.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:be7129a6dc7b6f71.summary: The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee is investigating a Russian oligarch's reported financial involvement in a celebration related to Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding , Axios has learned. Why it matters: Garcia is poised to be Congress' lead investigator if Democrats retake the House. This probe offers a pretty good hint of the direction he'll go in that role. "Oversight Democrats are investigating the numerous ways in which the Trump family have sought to enrich themselves on the basis of their proximity to President Donald Trump," Garcia stated in a letter to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. In a separate letter to Trump Jr. , Garcia wrote that ProPublica's reporting on Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev's role in funding the event "may be the most serious allegation against you to date." Driving the news: Kremlev, the president of the International Boxing Association, provided hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of expenses for the May party in the Bahamas, according to ProPublica. Kremlev is close to Russian President Vladimir Putin, and his boxing organization is financed by Russian state-owned energy company Gazprom. The oligarch paid for one of the two private islands where the event was held and a fireworks show, according to ProPublica, despite Trump Jr.'s estimated $300 million net worth . A Trump Jr. spokesperson did not dispute the payments to ProPublica, telling the outlet Kremlev is "a personal friend of Don," but "not someone he has a business relationship with." Kremlev's press office told ProPublica the two met "a couple of years ago" and "have a friendly relationship," and that he has "never discussed political matters with any of his American friends and acquaintances." Trump Jr.'s wife, Bettina Anderson, said in a statement on Instagram that it is "unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister," adding, "Friendship doesn't require a political motive." President Trump said in a…

33e1d7779a:3e5d5e16d0e7f882.title: Baal out: Top diplomat's worry about pagan god elicits eye rolls
33e1d7779a:3e5d5e16d0e7f882.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:3e5d5e16d0e7f882.summary: The second-most powerful man at the State Department put the brakes on a U.S. international exhibit featuring a bull statue because he worried it might look like Baal, a pagan god some associate with Satanic child sacrifice. Why it matters: The anecdote illustrates the quirky interests of Deputy Secretary of State Chris Landau, according to department critics, who say he spends too much time on social media focusing on the unimportant. Zoom in: The issue revolves around an international exposition next year in Belgrade, Serbia , where the U.S. plans to feature a statue of a bucking bull at an exhibit celebrating the American West. On Aug. 19, at 4:15 p.m., Landau sent an email to staffers about it: "I remain somewhat concerned by the Golden Bull imagery! Did a quick internet search and don't want it to become a distraction. The golden calf from the Bible is often portrayed as a golden bull." Providing hyperlinked footnotes and images of golden bull worship, Landau explored the ancient history of Baal as well as the "Modern Cultural Comparisons." "The imagery of a golden bull or calf is frequently invoked metaphorically today," he wrote. "For instance, critics and commentators sometimes compare modern financial fixations—typified by the famous Charging Bull statue on Wall Street to the ancient worship of material idols." Behind the scenes: The email, which was forwarded to multiple officials, elicited eyerolls and snickers inside the State Department. The bull statue was put on hold as State officials spent the last few weeks debating how to make it both interesting and non-Satanic. "It's just totally weird stuff and it's really indicative of the guy," a State Department official said. "Literally, no one thinks about Baal unless they're spending way too much time online, which Landau is," a different U.S. official lamented. "It's like an episode of Veep. Someone should tell him this is a Western bull, not a Near East bull," a third U.S. official said. Landau…

33e1d7779a:0de26086624a840f.title: Why a swift AI pause is unlikely: no one trusts AI companies
33e1d7779a:0de26086624a840f.author: Bradley Olson
33e1d7779a:0de26086624a840f.summary: Most agree the AI industry needs oversight. The critical barrier: Few really trust the industry, or the safety advocates who come from inside the house. Why it matters: Factions in the Trump administration, business executives wary of competitive threats, and advocates for cheaper, more customizable "open" models fear that new regulatory hurdles will offer frontier AI companies too much power. What they're saying: "I do not want a few humans in control of intelligence," Gavin Baker, a top tech investor and commentator on the AI race, said Sunday on X . Baker said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was surely sincere when he proposed new AI regulatory proposals in an essay Saturday , although the moves "would be good for his business over the long-term." Catch up quick : Four leading U.S. AI companies endorsed a potential pause in AI development this weekend after a series of troubling hacking incidents and awe-inducing displays of new model capabilities. The suggested pause caused a dip in global markets Monday as investors pondered what a slowdown in AI, one of the few reliable engines of economic growth this year, would do to economies around the world. Any hope of quick action extending from that fragile unity quickly shattered as critics spoke up and made clear just how much they distrust frontier AI players. AI distrust, explained Here are the key factors shaping that distrust, which are poised to delay the kind of "all-hands-on-deck" response many want. 💰Money : Anthropic stands alone in the history of capitalism, a company whose leaders are so concerned with safety that it broke away from OpenAI. Its employees, up to the CEO, honestly believe its product is so dangerous that there's a chance it could destroy humanity. And yet, as soon as this week, it's expected to file for what many expect will be the biggest IPO of all time, seeking to raise $100 billion at a $2 trillion valuation. Picture Oppenheimer meeting with sell-side analysts and you get a window into the…

33e1d7779a:04e1eda56ffb33a1.title: "I am the Hoax Buster": Trump's war on AI doomers gets personal
33e1d7779a:04e1eda56ffb33a1.author: Zachary Basu
33e1d7779a:04e1eda56ffb33a1.summary: President Trump declared war on the AI safety panic Monday, dismissing the industry's apocalyptic warnings as part of a "sick conspiracy" to sabotage America and his legacy. Why it matters: Trump is rewriting a complex, years-long debate over AI's dangers in the partisan grammar that has defined MAGA for a decade — hoaxes, conspiracies, traitors and, at the center of it all, one man. "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT," Trump wrote in a barrage of pro-AI Truth Social posts, where he accused Democrats of stoking the panic. State of play: Monday marked a sharp escalation in the administration's long-standing opposition to AI regulation, as Trump recast the safety debate in starkly personal terms. Trump explicitly placed AI doomerism in the same bucket as the Russia investigation , climate change and his impeachments — the latest entry in a catalog of "hoaxes" that has also included the Epstein files and the affordability crisis . He turned his fire on the AI leaders urging restraint, questioning why CEOs would seek regulations that could cripple their own companies and arguing that any slowdown would squander America's lead over China. The intrigue: Trump's campaign against AI doomerism then spilled onto the stage of the "All In Summit" in Los Angeles, where Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang took a call from the president in the middle of a live interview. Addressing thousands of tech executives, investors and founders on speakerphone, Trump dismissed fears of an AI takeover as a "hoax" and assured the crowd that "the robots will not be taking over." Screenshot via Truth Social Between the lines: Trump is grafting his own political grievances onto a counter-narrative already taking hold among his Silicon Valley allies: that the AI panic is manufactured. David Sacks, Trump's influential AI adviser and "All In" podcaster, has portrayed AI alarmism as the work of a well-funded " Doomer Industrial Complex " that includes…

33e1d7779a:6f5d7e6301e925f6.title: Supreme Court strikes down USPS mail-in voting rule
33e1d7779a:6f5d7e6301e925f6.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:6f5d7e6301e925f6.summary: The Supreme Court struck down the U.S. Postal Service's rule restructuring mail-in voting Monday, halting a major Trump administration priority. The big picture: The 7-2 decision is a major win for voting rights advocates and the states that challenged the administration's plan; it also reverses the Supreme Court's earlier green light for President Trump's mail-in voting order. The justices' prior unsigned order allowing the rule to proceed was not a ruling on the merits — but this time around, they decided the government is "unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge." The rule would require states to submit lists of eligible voters to USPS, and the agency would then verify that those voters were receiving mail-in ballots before sending them out. The rule also had strict requirements on envelope design. Driving the news: While the court rejected the administration's stance, at least one concurring justice disagreed on the merits of the case. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in a concurring opinion with fellow Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson that "there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority" but that applying the proposed rules would be "arbitrary and capricious" for the midterm elections as state and local officials "do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule." Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented in a separate opinion. In their opinion, they called the filings claiming harm by some plaintiffs "cryptic" and that the USPS has the authority to implement a rule because Congress has empowered it to do so. Zoom out: The decision is likely the final say on the rule during this election cycle, with even U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani saying from the bench earlier this month that it was unclear how the government would implement the plans with November just around the corner. Steven Monteith, executive vice president at the Postal Service, said in a declaration…

33e1d7779a:0553244f5e7be04e.title: Thune sees role for Congress on AI — Trump does not
33e1d7779a:0553244f5e7be04e.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:0553244f5e7be04e.summary: Majority Leader John Thune is asserting Congress' prerogative to act on AI — but he's urging a "light touch" even in the face of "consequential risks." Why it matters: On his first day back after a five-week break, Thune (R-S.D.) outlined his vision for congressional action on an issue President Trump has dismissed as a " hoax ." "Congress has a job to do," Thune said. "I think there are some potential consequential risks associated with AI," Thune told reporters when asked if he believes AI poses an existential threat to humanity. He added, "Guardrails there make sense to me" about cutting-edge, frontier AI models. But Thune also said that "there are always people who are creating a worst-case-scenario-type conversation out there." Driving the news: An AI panic is rippling through Congress, but mostly on the Democratic side, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) calling to "slow down the pace of development" of AI to avoid a potentially catastrophic outcome. Publicly, Trump is professing not to be concerned and insists that he should have the sole authority to regulate AI. "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," he posted on his Truth Social account Monday morning. Zoom out: Republicans aren't questioning Trump's ability to lead the country's approach to AI regulation, but they are suggesting that Congress has a role to play. And they aren't ruling out legislation. "So we may need to do something," Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said. "But there are existing guardrails, and corporate responsibility is a big part of this." Zoom in: Thune said he spoke with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) on Saturday night about their AI bill, which would force companies creating frontier AI models to guard against catastrophic risks and submit to federal oversight. Thune said he has been working with Commerce Chair Ted Cruz (R-Tex.) to reintroduce the bill "hopefully soon." House GOP…

33e1d7779a:f194f3824ccf7c41.title: Trump's $5,000 checks get chilly Senate GOP reception
33e1d7779a:f194f3824ccf7c41.author: Erin Davis
33e1d7779a:f194f3824ccf7c41.summary: Data: OMB ; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Visuals Senate Republicans are doubtful — and, in some cases, dismissive — of President Trump's proposal to give Americans $5,000 checks if Republicans keep control of Congress. Why it matters: Trump's proposal isn't dead on arrival. But Republicans aren't exactly lining up behind it either. "I am withholding judgment on the bill until I see their list of pay-fors," Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said. "I don't support going and borrowing $1.2 trillion to be able to write the checks." "I would need to see details on it," Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.) said. Sen. Steve Daines (R-Mont.) said he wasn't sure about the mechanics of the proposal but that he's "also worrying about $40 trillion in debt." "You know, there's no specific proposal out there," Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said. "And obviously, however that were to come together, Congress would have a big role in determining." Zoom in: There are two massive unknowns about the " Trump Dividend " that the president promised in Dallas last week: eligibility and price tag. Vice President Vance has suggested that wealthy Americans wouldn't receive the payment. If every "every adult citizen in the United States" were eligible, as Trump suggested, it could cost some $1.3 trillion. That would be more than three times what the U.S. collects annually from tariffs and other customs duties and fees. The intrigue: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), who frequently defers to Trump, said Sunday that Congress would have to approve the payments. Asked in NBC's "Meet the Press" if he'd commit that the checks will be sent, Johnson said, "I commit that Congress will work through it and find consensus on that like they have to do everything else." Rep. Keith Self (R-Texas) told Axios: "Well, if it happens, I'm recommending to people that they put it away in order to pay for the additional inflation. We will see." — Axios' Kate Santaliz contributed reporting for this story.

33e1d7779a:4e8be7ac90621d77.title: McConnell returns to Capitol after 3-month absence
33e1d7779a:4e8be7ac90621d77.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:4e8be7ac90621d77.summary: Sen. Mitch McConnell voted at the U.S. Capitol on Monday for the first time in three months after being hospitalized in June. Why it matters: The Kentucky Republican's return could finally unjam the farm bill — and put some MAGA world rumors to rest about his ability to do the job. McConnell arrived in a wheelchair and spoke briefly to reporters, joking that after years of avoiding their questions, he "wasn't sure how many of you would be here today. But I'm glad to see you. It's time to get back to work." He did not take questions but cast a vote Monday evening in favor of Matthew Byrne's nomination to be a district judge in Ohio. ' McConnell said he was ready to work on the farm bill, as well as on supporting NATO and Ukraine. Driving the news: " Today, I'll cast my first Senate vote since I took a bad fall back in June," McConnell said in a Monday evening statement. "I'm really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues." He described his recovery as "a long and often frustrating process," noting "the lingering effects of childhood polio haven't made it any easier." McConnell added, "I'm still not quite back to 100%, but I've assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me." What to watch: Whether the Senate Agriculture Committee will set a hearing this week to finally move the farm bill forward with McConnell's help. Catch up quick: McConnell, 84, was last seen at the Capitol on June 11. Since then, his team has provided few details about his health, fueling rampant online speculation. McConnell said in July that he fell at his home in June, briefly lost consciousness and was treated for mild pneumonia after he was hospitalized. The last official update came Aug. 6, when McConnell's office announced that he had been discharged from a rehabilitation facility and would continue recovering at home. Kentucky Gov.…

33e1d7779a:16ad119b8cbd3782.title: Trump DHS whistleblower alleges workers lied to access state voter data
33e1d7779a:16ad119b8cbd3782.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:16ad119b8cbd3782.summary: Department of Homeland Security employees were instructed to access state voter databases in ways a whistleblower alleges violate state law, according to a new report. Why it matters: The policy signals the Trump administration's persistence in trying to root out purported voter fraud by any means necessary. Driving the news: The whistleblower report , released by Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), details a protected whistleblower disclosure that "reveals serious allegations of illegal and inappropriate activities" within DHS' Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate. Employees have been asked to access sensitive voter information in state voter databases of people flagged by DHS as potential "unlawful voters," the report says. The whistleblower says the process can result in errors involving naturalized U.S. citizens, potentially subjecting them to secondary customs screenings at airports, or criminal referrals to Homeland Security Investigations. Zoom in: Some states, such as Virginia and Florida, require users signing onto the databases to legally confirm that they are the voter or an expressly authorized representative, meaning federal officers are effectively making false statements to access private records, the report says. Officers are also under tremendous pressure to review and verify a person's citizenship status in 12 minutes and enter it into a law enforcement record. The whistleblower says officers were told to rely on data they knew could be inaccurate, and employees' training on the new procedures amounted to a less-than-two-hour video. As a result, U.S. citizens are being investigated through the initiative "without their knowledge or ability to correct erroneous data," the report says. When officers questioned the practice, they were told individual officers would not be held personally liable for the searches, which the report says could indicate that the agency "is aware that the activity may be illegal."…

33e1d7779a:6768bd77a6d892a8.title: Trump and Jensen Huang unite against AI doomers in surprise on-stage call
33e1d7779a:6768bd77a6d892a8.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:6768bd77a6d892a8.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang took a surprise call from President Trump onstage at the All-In Summit Monday in Los Angeles, where the two dismissed fears of an AI takeover. Why it matters: Trump and Huang are staking out an increasingly clear rejection of AI doomerism right as some of the world's most powerful CEOs and AI experts call for slower AI development over safety concerns. Driving the news: Huang appeared to receive a call from Trump in the middle of an All-In Podcast interview Monday, according to video footage circulating on social media. Huang put the president on speaker so the crowd could hear the conversation. What they're saying: Trump and Huang shared an optimistic view of AI, highlighting its potential for economic growth and national security. "The robots will not be taking over," Trump told Huang. "The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax," he said, referring to the recent wave of warnings about catastrophic AI risks. Huang told Trump: "We're going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race of America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people." Zoom out: Huang separately addressed the AI safety fears that erupted over the weekend, striking a more nuanced tone than Trump. He said warnings from whistleblowers should be taken seriously, praising Anthropic whistleblower Jacob Coxon for having "great courage" to raise his concerns about the company's AI development going too quickly. Yes, but: Huang rejected predictions that AI could end the world as "not grounded in science." He said AI companies should pause or pace their work "if they feel that their company is out of control." The big picture: Huang has repeatedly dismissed AI doomer fears , suggesting that some cybersecurity alarm around AI can help drum up business for the security industry. "What better way to create demand than to create a problem," Huang said at a Goldman Sachs conference in San Francisco last week, per Forbes . "Who…

33e1d7779a:159fb727b127bb2a.title: "Look for other ways to get attention": House Dems face new Trump impeachment blowup
33e1d7779a:159fb727b127bb2a.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:159fb727b127bb2a.summary: Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) is facing swift and intense anger from his Democratic colleagues after announcing plans to force a vote to impeach President Trump this week. Why it matters: This is a messaging headache the party did not need going into the House's last week in session before midterm Election Day, frustrated House Democrats told Axios. "It's fucked up," said a senior House Democrat, speaking on the condition of anonymity to offer candid criticism of a fellow Democrat. Fumed a second lawmaker: "There's a reason why Al Green isn't coming back. This is exactly what people don't want.
