People want us focusing on affordability and AI, not on starting this futile impeachment game." Green said in an interview: "People are dying, and they are talking about strategy." Driving the news: Green said in a letter to Trump, which he cc'd to fellow members of Congress, that he will exercise his privilege to force a House impeachment vote "during the legislative business of September 14-17." He said the vote will be based on the killings of Renée Good , Alex Pretti , Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero by federal immigration officers. "You are condoning, supporting, and covering up these unjustified killings. The American people deserve more from their leader," Green wrote to Trump. Between the lines: Green, who lost his primary to fellow Rep. Christian Menefee (D-Texas) in May, has positioned himself as one of the president's most obdurate critics in Congress. He was escorted out of Trump's speech to a joint session of Congress last year and his State of the Union this year, both times for heckling. He mounted rogue efforts to impeach Trump in 2017 , 2018 , and twice last year , but all of his attempts were quashed in bipartisan procedural votes . What we're hearing: A third House Democrat vented that "Rep. Green appears to only be thinking about himself. Not about strategy. Not about building a coalition." "We need serious people in our caucus…

33e1d7779a:c77d40cd6ddc5481.title: Nationalist leaders say U.K. union "coming to an end"
33e1d7779a:c77d40cd6ddc5481.author: Rebecca Falconer
33e1d7779a:c77d40cd6ddc5481.summary: The first ministers of Northern Ireland , Scotland and Wales united Monday behind calls to leave the United Kingdom in an unprecedented alignment of nationalist leaders. Why it matters: For the first time, all three first ministers favor leaving the U.K. — and Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill says President Trump's support for a united Ireland has taken the debate global. Driving the news: The nationalist leaders of the Scottish National Party , Sinn Féin and Plaid Cymru met in Cardiff, Wales, on Monday to sign a memorandum of understanding declaring that the "political landscape across these islands is changing." The SNP's John Swinney, Sinn Féin's O'Neill and Plaid Cymru's Rhun ap Iorwerth met as leaders of their respective parties, not as representatives of their regional governments. Swinney and O'Neill called for referenda on independence from the U.K. during a news conference, but ap Iorwerth is pushing for similar regional powers as in Northern Ireland and Scotland and has ruled out holding a referendum during this term. What they're saying: "For people watching across these islands – for people watching around the world – there could be no clearer sign that Westminster's time is coming to an end," the memo said . "Momentum is behind our movements; we believe that constitutional change is coming," it added. "We call for the British Government to prepare for, plan and facilitate constitutional change in each jurisdiction." Zoom in: O'Neill told reporters that Trump's support for Irish reunification during a two-day visit over the weekend reflected a "growing conversation around constitutional change at home in Ireland." She said the debate was happening "not just at home, but obviously now internationally as well" and Trump's intervention showed Irish unification is "very much on the table." Yes, but: A spokesperson for U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Trump's comments don't change his stance that it's premature to call for…

33e1d7779a:29d908ed1eb5216e.title: Texas nominees' racist, vulgar remarks receive mixed GOP reaction
33e1d7779a:29d908ed1eb5216e.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:29d908ed1eb5216e.summary: Republicans have condemned, sidestepped or continued to support two Texas GOP nominees after one's racist post this weekend about students of color and another's years of vulgar comments about women sparked backlash. The big picture: In a fiercely heated midterm election, some candidates' racist, sexist and crude material online hasn't always been enough to cost them their party's support. Warning: This story includes crude, sexually explicit language that may disturb some readers. Driving the news: House Speaker Mike Johnson was asked Sunday on CNN about vulgar comments Brandon Herrera, a YouTuber-turned-candidate running for a key Texas district, made online in the past — including calling a Nazi submachine gun the "original ghetto blaster." In a 2023 clip played on CNN's "State of the Union" of Herrera addressing Moms Demand Action's Shannon Watts, he said, "Just because you let somebody cream-pie you doesn't mean I have to give a s--t about your political opinions. The fact that you kept your c-m trophy doesn't make you any less wrong about the dumb s--t that you say." Johnson, who campaigned for Herrera, called the language "detestable" — but applauded his "very effective campaign." He continued, "That was — that was his [YouTuber] persona online, right? Right now, he's running as a very serious candidate for Congress and a very thoughtful guy." Herrera is running for the seat ex - Rep. Tony Gonzales resigned in April after admitting to an affair with a staffer who later died by suicide. President Trump initially endorsed Gonzales but then threw his support behind Herrera. Zoom out: Bo French, the Republican nominee for the state's Railroad Commission, which regulates the gas industry, sparked outrage this weekend after sharing a photo of students of color celebrating at a Texas Longhorns' game. " I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn't believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined," French wrote in the post that,…

33e1d7779a:303f5598226c0bf6.title: Cities challenge Trump immigration rule over public benefits access
33e1d7779a:303f5598226c0bf6.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:303f5598226c0bf6.summary: New York City and five other Democratic-led local governments sued the Department of Homeland Security to block a new Trump administration rule they say will drive immigrants and mixed-status families away from public benefits they can legally receive. Why it matters: The cities warn the rule could drive hundreds of thousands out of health, food and housing programs , worsening public health , increasing homelessness and shifting millions of dollars in costs to local hospitals and governments. What they're saying: "The federal government has waged a campaign of violence and terror," New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a Monday news conference. "People could die as a result of these changes," he said. "… The data is clear: denying people services does not erase their need; it compounds it, generating a greater cost to our system that will be placed on the backs of working people for years to come. Nothing about this rule will reduce waste or keep Americans safer or improve New Yorkers' lives. It is simply a vehicle for confusion and a vehicle for cruelty." The White House and DHS did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Catch up quick: The administration's rule takes effect this week and gives immigration officers broader discretion to deny green cards and visas based on immigrants' use of public benefits. Plaintiffs say the change abandons a century-old standard that limited who was considered a "public charge" to people who are "primarily dependent" on government cash assistance. The cities and counties argue the new rule will deter immigrant families from using Medicaid, SNAP, and housing assistance programs. New York City, Chicago, San Francisco and Seattle, along with Santa Clara County, California, and King County, Washington, filed the suit. Zoom in: DHS estimates over 950,000 people might disenroll or decline to enroll in public benefits, though the plaintiffs allege that estimate probably understates the effect. The final rule…

33e1d7779a:d9aca1f1566a9e20.title: Trump says a strong, smart president is the only "guardrail" AI needs
33e1d7779a:d9aca1f1566a9e20.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:d9aca1f1566a9e20.summary: President Trump lashed out at calls for new AI guardrails and protections, arguing AI only needs a "STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT" and that AI critics should "BEWARE!" Why it matters: Trump continues to plant himself against calls for AI safety regulations as a growing chorus of AI leaders and CEOs call for a slowdown in AI's development and better regulations to help keep humanity safe. What he's saying: "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" Trump wrote on Truth Social . "WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so." This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:7b10be6cfc51f2ec.title: How Warsh can avoid a repeat of July's communications mess
33e1d7779a:7b10be6cfc51f2ec.author: Neil Irwin
33e1d7779a:7b10be6cfc51f2ec.summary: Seven weeks ago, Warsh took questions from the media, and it didn't go well . Markets sold off as he seemed vague and evasive about the reasoning behind the latest interest rate decision. Wednesday, he gets a do-over. Why it matters: Investors will be thirsty for a more detailed explanation of the Fed's decision than the one Warsh offered in late July — even while respecting his intention not to give explicit guidance about future policy moves. Markets are pricing in a quarter-point increase in rates — but the why behind that likely move is more significant than the act itself, for what it says about the Fed's analytical framework under its new leadership. And if the Fed's policymaking Federal Open Market Committee elects to leave rates unchanged, Warsh will have an even trickier communications task, lest the bond market again start to question Warsh's willingness to use interest rate policy to keep inflation in check. State of play: Assuming the Fed raises rates, does it reflect a belief that seemingly one-off changes to prices from tariffs and the energy shock are turning out to be more prolonged than previously thought? Or is AI-fueled investment creating more sustained inflationary pressure? Is it simply that the neutral interest rate is higher than it seemed? Not all interest rate adjustments are created equal. A "mid-cycle adjustment," like the three rate cuts enacted in 2019, or a "recalibration" or an "insurance move" imply different things from something like a "normalization" or a sustained policy tightening. Between the lines: Of course, each of these potential answers has implications for what the Fed will do next, in tension with Warsh's deeply held desire to avoid anything resembling "forward guidance." Moreover, different officials on the policy committee may have different rationales for a rate hike (or for not hiking), and as chairman Warsh has an obligation to accurately describe the range of views. But there's a pick-your-poison dilemma he…

33e1d7779a:92edc75de416adbf.title: Trump's USPS mail-ballot rules hit a second roadblock as Supreme Court weighs case
33e1d7779a:92edc75de416adbf.author: Andrew Pantazi
33e1d7779a:92edc75de416adbf.summary: A second federal judge blocked the U.S. Postal Service's new mail-ballot rules for the Nov. 3 midterms as the Supreme Court weighs whether to allow the restrictions in another case. Why it matters: Sunday's order adds another hurdle to the Trump administration's bid to upend mail voting . The blocked rules would allow the USPS to refuse ballots that don't clear new standards, with mail voting already underway in some states. The latest: U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, a Trump appointee in Washington, D.C., concluded Congress empowered the Postal Service to move mail, not to force states to enroll mail voters in a federal portal or to refuse ballots that fail its checks. Nichols' ruling follows a similar order from U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston blocking parts of the same rule. The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals left Talwani's injunction in place on Sept. 10. Talwani's order found the postal rules violate the U.S. Constitution and federal statute, while Nichols' new ruling relied entirely on his finding that Congress' Postal Reorganization Act doesn't allow many of the new rules. The White House and USPS did not immediately return requests for comment. Catch up quick: President Trump has long attacked mail voting, despite repeatedly using the method himself, including in August's Florida primaries . His March executive order directed the Postal Service to develop new envelope, tracking and voter-list requirements for mail voting. The Supreme Court already lifted an earlier injunction because the final rule hadn't been published yet. But after its publication, challengers returned to court and won new injunctions in Boston and D.C. The Trump administration is now asking the high court to stop Talwani's order and allow the new rules. Between the lines: Nichols said USPS might have the authority to issue rules on ballot-envelope designs, but he blocked the whole rule, finding its design, portal and rejection provisions too intertwined. Friction…

33e1d7779a:b89db9283116451f.title: Washington's AI paralysis: Let 'er rip vs. hit the brakes
33e1d7779a:b89db9283116451f.author: Zachary Basu
33e1d7779a:b89db9283116451f.summary: President Trump is as all-in on AI as a politician could be: all gas, no brakes, and zero interest in hand-wringing about dystopian risks or public disdain. Democrats are as conflicted on AI as a party could be: skeptical of the labs, spooked by their warnings, but split on whether to shut it all down. Why it matters: This staggering divide makes consensus on federal AI regulation almost unimaginable this year — and probably through early 2029, regardless of who wins control of Congress. Zoom in: Trump has governed as the AI president from Day 1 , applying the same doctrine to models and the data centers that power them — build faster, regulate less, beat China. Speaking in Ireland on Sunday, he dismissed new safety warnings as the work of "a lot of negative forces ... bringing up things that won't happen" — and reduced the stakes to one line: "Whoever wins AI wins." It's unclear which "negative forces" Trump has in mind: Calls to slow the race — or " pace the frontier " — are now coming from the leaders of America's premier AI labs, including Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google. Between the lines: Trump's accelerationist allies, including venture capitalists in Silicon Valley, see the safety alarms as a cynical ploy by the field's dominant players to lock in favorable regulations. David Sacks, Trump's former AI czar and a leading voice for the administration's hands-off approach, has a simple answer : Slow yourselves down. If OpenAI and Anthropic truly think the frontier is moving too fast, Sacks argues, they can decelerate on their own without using Washington to force competitors to do the same. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) echoed Sacks' argument that the labs don't need Congress to slow themselves down — and rejected calls for an emergency moratorium. Johnson said on NBC's "Meet the Press" that he'd recall the House and put AI regulation to a vote "if we had the solution," but warned Congress against rushing into rules it doesn't yet understand. His…

33e1d7779a:0f558b4b28ceb363.title: How Republicans secretly got Fetterman for their convention
33e1d7779a:0f558b4b28ceb363.author: Alex Isenstadt
33e1d7779a:0f558b4b28ceb363.summary: The biggest surprise of last week's Republican midterm convention began with an audacious request from the organizers to GOP Sen. Dave McCormick: Could he get Democratic Sen. John Fetterman, a fellow Pennsylvanian, to make an appearance? "I'll ask him," McCormick said. Within days, Fetterman — who's been increasingly at odds with the Democratic Party's liberal wing — was on board. Why it matters: Fetterman's 64-second video — calling himself a "common-sense Democrat," praising McCormick and vowing to work with President Trump to defend Pennsylvania's steel industry — represented Fetterman's biggest break yet with his party. Behind the scenes: According to three sources familiar with the talks, the idea for Fetterman to make the appearance emerged over the summer, as organizers of the Dallas convention sought what they called an "Oh sh*t" moment. They were looking to drive home a key midterm message — that Democrats are too extreme. Organizers discussed featuring "walk away" figures — people who had supported Democrats but had become disillusioned with the party. Republican operative Tony Sayegh, a leading convention organizer, was a driving force behind the idea, and Trump adviser Jason Miller backed the plan. Fetterman topped their list. Zoom in: Sayegh, a friend of McCormick's, took the idea to him in July. McCormick had developed a friendship with Fetterman as the Democrat grew more estranged from his party, particularly over many Democrats' criticism of Israel. Organizers knew getting Fetterman involved would be a massive coup. The intrigue: McCormick approached Fetterman carefully, knowing the backlash his Democratic colleague could face if he agreed to a role in the GOP convention. McCormick asked Fetterman to introduce him at the convention. A source said McCormick added: "I don't want you to do something that's not good for you." The two senators hashed it out over calls and texts for a few days. "I want to do it. I'm sure it will make people mad,"…

33e1d7779a:f12695e121249a04.title: Dems' primary plan gives Native Americans more power
33e1d7779a:f12695e121249a04.author: Holly Otterbein
33e1d7779a:f12695e121249a04.summary: The 2028 race for the White House will give new political clout to a long-overlooked constituency: Native American voters. Driving the news: New Mexico now holds an influential early spot as one of the first states to vote in the Democratic primary — on Feb. 15, 2028. That's put Native Americans , who make up about 12% of the state, in position to wield more influence in the presidential race than ever before. In recent Democratic primaries, New Mexico typically has voted late in the season, in June. States that held the earliest primaries had much smaller Native populations. Now potential presidential campaigns are scrambling to adjust to the 2028 lineup, calling Native leaders to learn about Indigenous power players and the dynamics of tribal governments, Democratic operatives tell Axios. Zoom in: Any presidential candidate who wants to win New Mexico is "going to have to listen to tribes," warned Deb Haaland, the former U.S. interior secretary who made history in 2021 when she became the first Native American to head a cabinet agency. "We could be a large part in who that nominee is." Native leaders and their allies say that will force presidential candidates to engage closely with tribal governments and pay attention to issues such as tribal sovereignty, land and water rights, and rural infrastructure. Several potential 2028 contenders are already taking notes. Isaac Dakota Casados, a New Mexico Democratic consultant and Navajo Nation member, told us his phone has been ringing off the hook as presidential campaigns-in-waiting look to learn more about Native voters. "They're really trying to figure out how the Native American demographic plays into this larger picture," he said. "I think they're used to speaking to Hispanic and Latino populations within their states. This is a very unique variable that's very different to them." Casados said Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker acknowledged to him that he's "really gotta learn" about tribal leadership, while New Jersey…

33e1d7779a:3a572b5882a9bd87.title: Trump's $5,000 checks require Congress to approve, Johnson says
33e1d7779a:3a572b5882a9bd87.author: Ben Berkowitz
33e1d7779a:3a572b5882a9bd87.summary: President Trump's proposal to send adult U.S. citizens $5,000 dividend checks would require congressional approval, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said on Sunday. Why it matters: Trump and his top officials claim they can send the checks without Congress — even with the prospect of them costing upward of $1.3 trillion. What they're saying: " He'd need Congress to act," Johnson said in a CNN interview. Asked by NBC's ""Meet the Press" if he'd commit that the checks will be sent, Johnson said "I commit that Congress will work through it and find consensus on that like they have to do everything else." Driving the news: President Trump, at the GOP's midterm convention in Dallas, said this week he'd order a $5,000 check — a "Trump Dividend" — if Republicans retained control of the House and the Senate. Trump and other officials have said the dividend would be funded by tariffs, gains on investments and other income. The president told reporters before departing Ireland on Sunday that "the $5,000 checks are going forward" and that he had thought of this plan "a while ago." When a reporter asked why not do the checks now instead of after the midterm elections, given Republicans currently control Congress, Trump replied: "Because if the Democrats get in, our country will be in shambles." The big picture: Such a massive stimulus also comes with significant economic risks , both to the deficit and inflation. The idea has already met bipartisan opposition, though Trump has insisted the offer and the checks will happen. Editor's note: This story has been updated with new details throughout.

33e1d7779a:b6358e4ec96df61f.title: Why Trump's united Ireland stance hit such a nerve
33e1d7779a:b6358e4ec96df61f.author: Rebecca Falconer
33e1d7779a:b6358e4ec96df61f.summary: President Trump stood by his support for a united Ireland on Sunday after his remarks during a two-day visit sparked a backlash from unionist and British politicians and praise from Irish nationalists. Why it matters: Trump broke with a longstanding U.S. presidential convention of not taking sides on whether Northern Ireland should ultimately be British or Irish. The U.S. helped broker the 1998 Good Friday Agreement , built around consent and parity between British unionism and Irish nationalism. Former President Clinton, whose administration played a central role in the peace process , explicitly said the U.S. was "neither in favor of a united Ireland nor opposed to the idea." Driving the news: Trump said in Dublin, sitting beside Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin on Saturday, that he'd "love to see" Ireland unified and that it is "going to happen eventually," so it "may as well happen now." He described uniting Northern Ireland with the Republic of Ireland as "fantastic," adding: "The U.K. would have something to say about it obviously, but I think it would be a great thing, I mean, how can it be bad?" Trump later said Irish reunification would be a "very cool thing" while noting that "no matter what you say or how you say it, there's no good answer." On Sunday, Trump told reporters: "It just seems to me that you have Northern Ireland and you have Ireland. It seems to me that one of the naturals of all time is to put them together." He added this was only his opinion, but "many people agree" and he "had so much support" in response to his remarks. Between the lines: Trump has managed the unusual feat of delighting Irish nationalists while alarming some Northern Irish politicians who have previously expressed support for him. Martin revealed that Trump has privately expressed the same preference before. What they're saying: While Irish nationalist politicians seized on Trump's comments and said "the conversation on Irish unity has shifted," unionists in Northern…

33e1d7779a:129a23f4b948ef99.title: Johnson calls for AI solutions but says Congress won't take the lead
33e1d7779a:129a23f4b948ef99.author: Donica Phifer
33e1d7779a:129a23f4b948ef99.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said Sunday that Congress won't lead the charge on regulating AI safety . Why it matters: Calls for AI companies to adopt safety protocols reached a fever pitch this week, prompting the four biggest AI labs to endorse slowing their models' development. Driving the news: Johnson was urged this week to cancel the House recess and bring representatives back to D.C. to pass a law on AI safeguards. During a Sunday appearance on CNN's "State of the Union," Johnson said Congress intervening isn't the answer and that AI companies can halt their work at any time. We have to "resist Congress jumping in and imposing some sort of emergency moratorium. It's got to be done right, safely, wisely. In a separate appearance on NBC's "Meet the Press," Johnson conceded that he would recall House members and schedule a vote on AI regulation "if we had a solution," but said any action from Congress must be done carefully. "We have to put up some guardrails, some safety measures in place to ensure that AI doesn't run away ....But at the same time, we've got to make sure that we don't lose our edge in the global competition on this with China. Because that would be a national security threat." What they're saying: Johnson told CNN and NBC he would like to organize a meeting between President Trump , members of Congress, and the top AI officials who call the shots at their respective companies. Johnson added to CNN that he would prefer AI company leaders to take a leadership role and responsibility for ensuring the safety of their products, rather than pushing Congress to implement rules. Johnson's comments mirror former White House AI czar David Sacks, who said late Saturday that the major labs should simply pace development on their own, without the government having to intervene. The other side: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) told ABC's "This Week" that Democrats planned to meet Tuesday morning to discuss AI. "We should take decisive…

33e1d7779a:cc0d45cace722565.title: AI's most powerful CEOs hit the brakes
33e1d7779a:cc0d45cace722565.author: Ben Berkowitz
33e1d7779a:cc0d45cace722565.summary: In nine startling hours on Saturday, the four biggest AI labs — which rarely agree on anything — set aside years of feuds and competition to endorse a slower development pace for their models. Their new stance: Prioritize safety over growth , even at a cost. The big picture: AI's unrelenting growth has hit an inflection point with the public, Washington and even the companies building it. Data centers are unpopular . People are panicked about doom scenarios . And 51 days before midterms, legislators suddenly realize there are points to be won by cracking down. Against that backdrop , the industry's most powerful CEOs hit the brakes Saturday. At 10 a.m. ET, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei dropped a 3,800-word essay saying model development needs to be paced , otherwise doom scenarios are possible — like a rogue-agent takeover of the entire internet, which he said could be as soon as six months from now. An hour later, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk shocked the AI chattering class by quoting Amodei's essay on X and saying "Dario is right." Musk — who heads SpaceXAI, formerly xAI — had pointedly not joined previous industry-wide calls for any kind of slowdown. At 12:30 p.m., OpenAI CEO Sam Altman tweeted: "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier." In an interview Friday that was released on Saturday, Altman told Fortune his company won't go public this year, dashing hopes for a blockbuster IPO. He said OpenAI has too much safety work to do and would be better off doing that as a private company. At 7 p.m., Demis Hassabis — the Nobel laureate who co-founded and chairs Google DeepMind, and is Alphabet's chief scientist — tweeted : "Dario's essay points towards the right path forward. The details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment." Between the lines: Publicly putting safety ahead of technological or financial growth may be the industry's only route to avoid a crackdown that's not on its terms. Legislators are begging House…

33e1d7779a:b1d9c1c9826aa552.title: The tab is coming due for America's borrowing binge
33e1d7779a:b1d9c1c9826aa552.author: Neil Irwin
33e1d7779a:b1d9c1c9826aa552.summary: Americans are facing a rising tab as a multi-decade borrowing binge collides with a spike in energy prices caused by the Iran war. The big picture: Long-term interest rates are surging, as are consumer prices. It's a toxic mix of near-term inflation pressures and years of fiscal imbalance. Driving the news: The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note rose to 4.97% Friday, up a full percentage point since the end of February, and only a hair below its high since 2007. The rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage has risen in lockstep, reaching 7.08% Friday, per Mortgage News Daily — the highest in more than a year. State of play: The immediate catalyst Friday was an inflation report that showed consumer prices surging higher in August, with gasoline prices accounting for more than a third of the gain. Gasoline is now at a national average of $4.29 a gallon, while the price of diesel has climbed to over $6 a gallon. All this means that the Federal Reserve is now expected to raise its target interest rate this week. But longer-term borrowing rates are set in global markets — and determined by bigger forces. The U.S. government is spending about $2 trillion a year more than it raises in taxes at a time the cumulative debt is already roughly 100% of a year's GDP. Long-term bond yields have been rising worldwide, reflecting both high government borrowing and demand for capital from the AI buildout. The intrigue: The recent spikes have taken place in spite of interventions by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to try to smooth turbulent bond markets — efforts that haven't succeeded in making borrowing cheaper. And rather than focus on the deficit reduction the bond market wants, President Trump has floated the notion of $5,000 payments to all U.S. adult citizens if Republicans win midterm elections. The U.S. government is already spending around $1 trillion a year in interest on the debt, on track to rise to $2 trillion over the next decade, a new high as a share of…

33e1d7779a:970d140d5d8de83f.title: OpenAI delaying IPO amid AI safety concerns, Sam Altman says
33e1d7779a:970d140d5d8de83f.author: Donica Phifer
33e1d7779a:970d140d5d8de83f.summary: OpenAI will not go public this year given all the safety work it needs to do, CEO Sam Altman said in a Fortune interview released Saturday. Why it matters: Altman's comments come as fears over doomsday AI scenarios have ramped up since an Anthropic employee resigned and issued a dire warning about AI's capabilities. What they're saying: "Right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public," Altman said . "I would say not 2026, yeah. We got a lot of stuff to do," Altman told Fortune editor-in-chief Alyson Shontell. "Meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together, I'm happy to be able to do that as a private company." The intrigue: The market expected blockbuster IPOs from both OpenAI and Anthropic this year. Altman's move puts the ball squarely in Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's court — especially given Amodei's warning Saturday that AI development needs to be slowed. The bottom line: " I think a key principle that we should all agree on is that we cannot take actions that would risk losing control of the future to AI," Altman said. That means investors may have to wait a while. Editor's note: This story has been updated with new information throughout.

33e1d7779a:acb56bcccc09a602.title: Anthropic, OpenAI CEOs call for slowdown in AI development
33e1d7779a:acb56bcccc09a602.author: Ben Berkowitz
33e1d7779a:acb56bcccc09a602.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is calling for an immediate slowdown in the pace of AI development, warning of potentially devastating consequences in a matter of months otherwise. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman quickly agreed that the industry needs to slow the pace of frontier-model advances and take more steps on safety. Why it matters: Amodei pulled no punches in a new essay , cautioning that swarms of rogue AI agents could take over the internet in as little as six months from now. The big picture : This is the week that the AI safety debate broke into the public consciousness, driven by an Anthropic employee's very public resignation and warning of possible doom . Amodei's essay isn't necessarily a direct response, but it will have much the same effect amid a sudden surge of public and congressional outrage. What they're saying : "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain," Amodei wrote. "The measures I propose to advance the frontier at a safe pace will not be easy. But I believe we owe it to humanity to try." Threat level : He also specifically referenced the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face rogue agent incident , which he said could have been far worse. "Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails," he warned. Zoom out : Amodei said Anthropic would unilaterally take one key safety measure — giving external evaluators employee-level access to ensure safety procedures and report incidents. He called on the rest of the industry to do the same. He also called for coordination among democratic countries to establish safety standards, and an effort…

33e1d7779a:cbaabe5f98238302.title: Anthropic report: 5 ways Claude was exploited for war, spying and repression
33e1d7779a:cbaabe5f98238302.author: Zachary Basu
33e1d7779a:cbaabe5f98238302.summary: The AI safety debate exploded this week over warnings that the technology could one day destroy humanity. Anthropic's latest threat report offers a more immediate wake-up call: Today's models are already helping U.S. adversaries develop kamikaze drones, hunt dissidents and conduct dangerous virus research . Why it matters: AI is tearing down barriers that have long constrained the world's most dangerous actors. A handful of people can now mount operations that once required legions of spies, engineers or hackers. Driving the news: Anthropic — the safety-focused lab behind Claude — says it spent the past eight months tracking and disrupting attempts to misuse its models. Among the most alarming cases it uncovered: 1. An Iran-linked operation used Claude to help target U.S. naval forces. Claude helped build targeting handbooks tracking ship positions, U.S. personnel, aircraft and ship identifiers, satellite imagery and websites exposing naval movements. Other Iran-linked operations tapped the model for propaganda, domestic surveillance and targeting opposition figures and minorities. 2. Claude served as an engineer for a Yemeni team building missiles. A weapons cell in northern Yemen relied on Claude Code to develop guidance software for rockets and missiles. The team had separate copies write code, conduct research and check one another's work. After one guided-rocket test apparently failed, they returned to Claude within hours to diagnose what went wrong. 3. A China-linked operation used Claude to hunt Uyghurs . Anthropic says the actor sifted through more than 100 WhatsApp groups and dozens of Telegram channels to identify Uyghurs in Syria who could be pressured or paid to report on armed Uyghur groups. Claude then helped a non-Arabic-speaking operator carry out covert outreach in Syrian Arabic — translating replies and coaching efforts to exploit money problems, family separation and relatives still in Xinjiang. 4. One man used Claude to help build surveillance…

33e1d7779a:1a826e37682c6aa6.title: Behind the Curtain: It's not too late
33e1d7779a:1a826e37682c6aa6.author: Jim VandeHei
33e1d7779a:1a826e37682c6aa6.summary: The White House, Congress and the country's leading AI companies have allowed AI to grow faster, stronger, more powerful and wildly lucrative (and dangerous), with no serious effort to control it or spread the benefits beyond the super-wealthy. It's not too late to change this. But if they all dither, duck or dance around it, the chances of AI worst-case scenarios will explode, likely early next year, according to almost every person we talk to privately who truly understands AI. Why it matters: The technology is getting better, faster than anyone envisioned — with the possibility rising that AI will self-improve and do wildly unpredictable things. The good news: There's now a growing public cry for attention and action and, at least in private, a broad understanding of what could be done relatively fast with bipartisan and industry buy-in. The big picture: In July, I wrote an essay for The Wall Street Journal saying America "faces one of those rare, historic moments when government, business, schools and families could be working together to meet a truly generational challenge: winning the AI race. So far, we're blowing it." Two short months later, the technology is vastly better — and the societal response vastly dumber. As a nation, we're choosing to amuse or distract ourselves . Here's how to change that fast, based on our months of conversations with lawmakers, White House officials and AI labs. Think of what follows as me channeling their private views: Sound an all-hands-on-deck alarm. Every political topic is trivial and small compared to AI. We will look back in shame if we get spooled up about trans bans or $5,000 checks when countless AI insiders are warning of catastrophic outcomes. Let's say they're all paranoid and delusional. If so, it still doesn't matter: we've never seen this much investment in one technology this fast in human history. It's seeping into every industry and every job and every community and every screen, at a speed never before…

33e1d7779a:8fbfb750b6810250.title: The world reconsiders America
33e1d7779a:8fbfb750b6810250.author: Neal Rothschild
33e1d7779a:8fbfb750b6810250.summary: America is shedding its status as the default choice for foreign governments to park money, buy weapons and send students. Why it matters: Even modest shifts away from the U.S. could chip away at advantages that have helped sustain American economic and geopolitical power for decades. Driving the news: The Netherlands moved 86 tons of gold out of the U.S. and Canada last week, citing the move as a hedge against "extreme systemic risks." France already moved all of its gold out of New York, while Germany debated doing the same. Norway's sovereign wealth fund — the world's largest — announced plans to reduce its holdings of U.S. government bonds amid turbulence in the Treasury market. The big picture: Beyond finance, European countries are looking for ways to wean off the U.S. On weapons, Europe is seeking to source more equipment locally to reduce its dependence on American firepower, Reuters reports. On technology, the EU this summer set out plans to reduce its reliance on American companies, drafting cloud rules that would restrict Amazon, Google and Microsoft from competing for sensitive contracts, Reuters also reported . Zoom out: Individuals around the world are also recalibrating their relationship to the U.S. International applications to U.S. colleges dropped 10% in the most recent admissions cycle. Stricter international student visa policies and the Trump administration's broader immigration posture have weighed heavily. International travel to the U.S. fell 5.5% in 2025, the first decline since the pandemic, as relationships with longtime allies grew strained. Canadian travel dropped 25% last year, with the slide continuing into early 2026. German travel to the U.S. has dropped 25% since the beginning of Trump's term, with the country's travel association pointing to politics as one factor. By the numbers: America's standing has been hit especially hard in the West, according to a recent Pew study . Hungary and Poland were the only two of 10 countries…

33e1d7779a:16d6a86a0a88d10a.title: Jewish institutions' security spending tops $1 billion as antisemitism persists
33e1d7779a:16d6a86a0a88d10a.author: Russell Contreras
33e1d7779a:16d6a86a0a88d10a.summary: Antisemitic threats have pushed the nationwide cost of protecting Jewish synagogues, schools and community centers past $1 billion a year, new estimates reveal as congregations prepare for big crowds during the High Holy Days , which began Friday with Rosh Hashanah. Why it matters: Enhanced security has become a growing expense for Jewish communities, congregation leaders say, often taking up money that could pay for teachers, summer camps, elder care and other programs. By the numbers: Jewish communal institutions are now spending an estimated $1.02 billion annually on security, a record high, according to new data from the Jewish Federations of North America (JFNA). That's up 33% from the federation's previous annual estimate of $765 million in 2024. More than 4,500 synagogues, Jewish community centers, schools, summer camps and other nonprofits spend an average of roughly $225,000 each, the group said. Security personnel — including guards and security directors — account for the largest share. Of that total, about $150 million goes toward security technology and the "hardening" of buildings — upgrades that can include security cameras, reinforced doors and controlled-entry systems — as well as maintaining existing security equipment. The estimate doesn't include security costs at more than 1,600 kosher restaurants, about 500 kosher markets and groceries, and other privately owned Jewish businesses. State of play: Synagogues are increasingly moving beyond security guards and cameras to layered, year-round systems that include hardened entrances , trained congregants as security personnel and coordination with police. More than 7,100 volunteers now help protect more than 500 synagogues and events each week, according to Community Security Service (CSS) , a nonprofit that now protects more than 500 synagogues across the U.S. The expanded security comes as assaults linked to antisemitism have reached their highest level since the Anti-Defamation League began…

33e1d7779a:9aa54449199b9872.title: Record diesel prices stoke food inflation, transportation costs
33e1d7779a:9aa54449199b9872.author: Nathan Bomey
33e1d7779a:9aa54449199b9872.summary: The record price of diesel threatens to stoke inflation at a time when consumers are already price-sensitive and businesses are reeling from higher costs due to trade tensions. Why it matters: Diesel is a key cost throughout the supply chain, meaning soaring prices could eventually show up in what consumers pay for everything from groceries to household goods. Driving the news: The national average price of a gallon of diesel topped $6 for the first time ever, AAA said Friday, Axios' Ben Berkowitz reports . That's up 60% from a year earlier. Between the lines: Food prices could be among the first places consumers feel the ripple effects, executives said this week. At grocery chain Kroger, which has been trying to keep a lid on prices: "I would expect that the pressure is actually going to mount," CEO Greg Foran said Friday on an earnings call. At pork producer Smithfield Foods: "That impact is beginning to flow through in the second half of the year," CFO Mark Hall said Thursday. At Hormel Foods: "With the Iran war and the spike in diesel costs, that's been something we've had to confront," interim CEO Jeffrey Ettinger said Wednesday. But the effects extend well beyond food. For example, at Newell Brands — whose portfolio includes Rubbermaid, Sharpie and Coleman — the inflationary impacts of energy costs have far exceeded the company's initial estimates. "It's either resin, which is obviously dependent on the price of oil, or it is direct transportation costs, i.e., diesel," CFO Mark Erceg said Tuesday. The big picture: Energy prices have spiked since President Trump launched the war with Iran, which prompted the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping lane. The latest Energy Information Administration outlook expects retail diesel to average $4.40 a gallon in 2027, up 33 cents, or 8.2%, from its previous forecast of $4.07, Axios' Rebecca Falconer and Ben Geman reported . The average price of unleaded gasoline has also spiked, rising by $1.11 over the last…

33e1d7779a:a77cd5e4121bfaee.title: 9/11 widow blasts Saudi Arabia during annual ceremony
33e1d7779a:a77cd5e4121bfaee.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:a77cd5e4121bfaee.summary: A widow of a 9/11 victim used the annual reading of the names of those killed to plead with the Trump administration about Saudi Arabian officials' alleged ties to the terror attack, which the kingdom has dismissed. The big picture: During the New York City ceremony for 9/11's 25th anniversary, Terry Strada slammed Saudi Arabia, which Axios' Barak Ravid reports is actively urging President Trump to assist them with U.S. military action. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) and Trump have maintained a close relationship, while 9/11 families have expressed discomfort over U.S. officials' past engagement with Saudi Arabia. Driving the news: "For 25 years, administration after administration, including leaders in front of us here today, chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with the 9/11 families," Strada said during the ceremony. "It has been one betrayal after another. President Trump can still change that," she said. "Tell the Saudis to stop lying. Tell them that if they want to be friends with the USA, they cannot continue to deny all of this, all of the pain, all of the destruction that we have all been suffering through." She thanked Vice President Vance for attending the ceremony and urged him to "carry that message back." Another man participating in reading the names of the victims also appealed to Trump to "release the unredacted files that implicate Saudi Arabia while what's left of the victims' families are still alive to see it." Catch up quick: The oil-rich nation has long fought ongoing claims from victims' families, but last year, a federal judge determined that enough evidence existed to infer the kingdom employed two operatives to assist the hijackers, Axios' Marc Caputo previously reported. Families have pressed the Trump administration to declassify more government records. "We've seen him do it for the JFK files. Why not the 9/11 files?" Brett Eagleson, whose father was killed on 9/11, recently asked ABC News. Between the lines:…

33e1d7779a:eac61839798e979f.title: Afghan woman deported in first-ever "Alien Terrorist" court case, DOJ says
33e1d7779a:eac61839798e979f.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:eac61839798e979f.summary: An Afghan national who was the first-ever case before the federal Alien Terrorist Removal Court has been deported, the Justice Department announced Friday. The big picture: The DOJ win before the previously dormant court could give the administration a path to remove people it links to terrorism while keeping much of its evidence secret, Axios previously reported. "It'll be interesting to see what they do next," says Jess Dawgert, a former DOJ attorney and now founding partner at a firm focused on federal immigration litigation. "I can't imagine that now that they've done this and got this confession fairly quickly that they're not going to use it again." Driving the news: Chief Judge Joan Ericksen directed the removal of Nazira Haji Zada, a lawful permanent resident whom the government accused of assisting her son and son-in-law's foiled 2024 shooting plot, in a recently unsealed August 20 order. The DOJ said "the government used classified information to establish that Zada is an alien terrorist" and that Zada accepted that designation and waived appeal of the removal order. Zada's lawyers had previously argued the government violated her due process rights. "This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement. Catch up quick: The unclassified summary filed in the case accused Zada of being an ISIS supporter who worked to "radicalize the family" and backed her son and son-in-law's conspiracy. It further said the underlying information was classified "because disclosure would enable terrorists and terrorist organizations to avoid preventative or detection measures" or could reveal FBI or other intelligence sources. What they're saying: Zada's public defenders, Mary Petras and Matthew Farley, said in a statement to Axios that her "choice to consent to removal should not be seen as an endorsement of this court's…

33e1d7779a:5215c2fd370a05c2.title: Scoop: Mike Johnson urged to cancel House recess over AI warnings
33e1d7779a:5215c2fd370a05c2.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:5215c2fd370a05c2.summary: A letter is circulating among House members urging Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to bring back the House "immediately" and keep it in session until Congress passes AI safeguards , Axios has learned. Why it matters: Such drastic action has been proposed by members of both parties this week after current and former Anthropic researchers went public with warnings that AI could kill off humanity in the next decade. The letter to Johnson, drafted by Sam Liccardo (D-Calif.), says "urgent action" is needed "to address catastrophic risk posed by advanced artificial intelligence," according to a copy first obtained by Axios . The letter is co-signed by Reps. George Whitesides (D-Calif.), Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) and Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) but was still being circulated as of Friday afternoon. Driving the news: The letter calls for the House to "return to Washington immediately and remain in session until Congress advances meaningful, bipartisan AI safeguards." It notes that the House, which reconvenes Monday, is scheduled to be in session just one more week before departing for a month and a half, returning Nov. 9. "You can forgive every American who believes that Congress remains unserious about confronting our nation's most pressing challenges," the letter says. Reality check: Despite growing urgency from rank-and-file members to respond to the existential threat allegedly posed by AI, congressional leadership has largely offered up silence. Johnson is planning a vote next week on a bill to prevent data centers from driving up Americans' energy costs but has offered no indication that the House will vote on any AI regulations before Election Day. A spokesperson for Johnson did not provide comment. Between the lines: The letter points to the myriad bipartisan bills that have been proposed to regulate AI, arguing they "deserve consideration, public debate, thoughtful amendment, and action." They include the AI Kill Switch Act , introduced by Lieu and Rep. Nathaniel Moran…

33e1d7779a:defd995c243ff479.title: Contractor undercuts Trump's Reflecting Pool vandal claims
33e1d7779a:defd995c243ff479.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:defd995c243ff479.summary: The contractor hired to renovate the Reflecting Pool says its repair work caused the pool's liner to peel and bubble, according to documents first reviewed by The New York Times. Why it matters: President Trump has repeatedly blamed vandals for the pool's damage and has pushed to prosecute some of them, even after U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro dropped the cases . Driving the news: The contractor, Atlantic Industrial Coatings, admitted that both the design and execution of the renovation were flawed, according to the Times. Workers didn't spray enough primer in some areas to bond the liner's layers, but the "human oversight" wasn't as big a problem as the liner's chemical mixture. The two chemicals the contractor combined for the liner were incompatible. The top layer got so hot that the material underneath couldn't handle the heat, causing it to blister and peel away, the documents show. The two chemicals are rarely mixed, so the contractor wasn't aware of the incompatibility. Atlantic Industrial Coatings did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. What they're saying: "President Trump promised to make D.C. safe and beautiful, and he's delivering," a White House spokesperson told Axios in an emailed statement. "For years, the Reflecting Pool sat neglected, plagued with algae, and leaking millions of gallons of water. Fixing it was common sense. It's another example of President Trump restoring our nation's capital for the American people." Zoom in: An Interior Department spokesperson told Axios that crews are replacing deteriorating water valves, flushing clogged pipes, sealing leaks, pressure-washing sidewalks and cleaning the pool's granite coping stones. They also continued to blame vandals for some of the damage to the pool, saying that "the major vandalism of long razor-blade gashes" means that Atlantic Industrial Coating is replacing "the sections of the pool damaged by vandals, who also repeatedly reached into the pool and ripped at the…

33e1d7779a:8578be863a6f237d.title: CDC declares cyclospora outbreak over
33e1d7779a:8578be863a6f237d.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:8578be863a6f237d.summary: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention declared the cyclospora outbreak related to Taylor Farms lettuce over Friday, though the Food and Drug Administration says its investigation remains ongoing. The big picture: Thousands of people fell ill as the outbreak rapidly surged throughout the country this summer as federal authorities searched for its origin amid a backdrop of overlapping food safety investigations . Driving the news: " This outbreak has ended. The number of recent infections linked to the outbreak has significantly declined," the CDC said in a Friday update, noting the "contaminated lettuce linked to this outbreak is no longer available in stores or restaurants." The CDC currently lists 12,883 cases, 570 hospitalizations and two deaths across 21 states. Taylor Farms, a large retail and restaurant supplier, recalled lettuce sourced from central Mexico in connection with the outbreak. The outbreak also included people who reported eating at Taco Bell, which removed the affected Taylor Farms lettuce. Between the lines: Health officials stressed the challenge of tracking the tiny parasite because of the short shelf life of fresh produce and the lengthy incubation period before symptoms appear. The FDA said it is continuing its investigation into the outbreak linked to Taylor Farms de Mexico iceberg lettuce and the root cause of the outbreak. Zoom out: This summer saw a flurry of recalls and FDA investigations, colliding with a brewing grocery price shock . On top of the cyclospora outbreak, Salmonella surges triggered jalapeño and egg recalls, E. coli and Salmonella infections were linked to alfalfa sprouts, and powdered infant formula was pulled from shelves after cases of infant botulism — among other outbreaks. Food-safety advocates have expressed concerns about declining federal surveillance after the Trump administration eliminated or pushed out thousands of workers across the CDC, FDA and USDA, Axios' Josephine Walker previously reported. Go…

33e1d7779a:36b483fdfc85f247.title: Saudi crown prince urged Trump to strike Houthis amid Red Sea threat
33e1d7779a:36b483fdfc85f247.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:36b483fdfc85f247.summary: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) called President Trump twice Thursday, urging him to launch strikes against the Houthis as the Iran-backed group closed in on a vital Red Sea chokepoint, two U.S. officials told Axios. Trump declined, and U.S. officials stressed the administration has no plans to intervene directly against the Houthis for now. Why it matters: Oil prices surged Thursday as the Houthis seized a strategic coastal city in Yemen, pushing them closer to the Bab al-Mandab Strait — a vital artery for global trade and Saudi oil exports. With Iran already disrupting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz , Houthi control of Bab al-Mandab could give Tehran a powerful new point of leverage over the U.S. and its Gulf allies. The latest: Reuters reported Friday morning that the Houthis had taken control of a key island in the strait. They also reported that smoke was seen over the key east-west Saudi oil pipeline, though the source was not clear. Driving the news: The U.S. is concerned about the rapidly escalating fight in Yemen and is stepping up support for Saudi Arabia while trying to avoid direct military involvement. Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of U.S. Central Command, traveled to Saudi Arabia on Thursday for urgent coordination meetings, two sources with knowledge of the matter said. The Saudi embassy in Washington and the White House declined to comment. Catch up quick: The Saudi-Houthi confrontation reignited in July after Riyadh prevented an Iranian plane carrying senior Houthi officials home from the funeral of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei from landing in Sanaa. MBS asked Trump for political backing to strike the Sanaa airport, but made clear Saudi Arabia did not need U.S. military assistance. Trump gave him his support. The Houthis retaliated by attacking Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, threatening a crucial route for the kingdom's oil exports, and later expanded their attacks to Saudi energy facilities. 33e1d7779a:1218f61147e92676.title: How AI makes biological research more dangerous
33e1d7779a:1218f61147e92676.author: Caitlin Owens
33e1d7779a:1218f61147e92676.summary: This week's dire warnings about unchecked artificial intelligence destroying humanity are refocusing attention on how models already are being used in dangerous bioscience experiments — and the lack of safeguards. Why it matters: There's growing alarm about emerging risks from advances like AI-designed viruses. But it's hard to erect guardrails when there's no ironclad way of even knowing how some AI systems will act. AI-enabled bioweapons are one of the worst-case scenarios researchers have raised for the kind of catastrophic danger that could wipe out humanity. Driving the news: On Thursday, Anthropic disclosed that it disrupted five potential instances of actors using its models in ways that could support the development of biological weapons. The disclosure came in a threat assessment detailing real-world case studies it uncovered and disrupted between December and August. In two of the cases, researchers were attempting to use Claude for assistance with gain-of-function research on dangerous viruses — research that enhances pathogens in a lab to better understand them and their potential for starting pandemics. The assessment notes that biological capabilities can be used for beneficial or harmful purposes, and that it's difficult to determine intent, especially when sophisticated actors can hide their motives. "We take these cases as evidence not of the imminence of biological threats currently uplifted by Claude, but rather as evidence that significant dual-use research efforts are associated with state actors of concern who routinely evade our access controls," the report concludes. "Safeguarding access to such content will necessarily require account and institutional signals to verify user legitimacy, and the rudimentary observability provided by data retention to identify misuse." Anthropic's most recent models have been launched with safeguards that restrict access to biological research queries that could be misused. The big picture: The assessment…

33e1d7779a:760d5c186e1f4742.title: Inside the RNC's legal fight over "election integrity"
33e1d7779a:760d5c186e1f4742.author: Brittany Gibson
33e1d7779a:760d5c186e1f4742.summary: Less than two months before the midterms , Republicans are fighting roughly 200 legal battles to try to impact elections, including several cases in which the GOP isn't officially participating but is paying legal fees or advising on strategy. Driving the news: The Republican National Committee's vast roster of cases includes efforts to tighten voter ID rules in Montana, decrease ballot drop-off locations in Georgia, increase scrutiny of voter lists in New Jersey and Delaware, and boost access for election observers and challengers elsewhere. Five RNC officials described the scope of the party's nationwide "election integrity" effort to Axios. They said strict enforcement of voting laws and preventing noncitizens from registering and voting are top priorities — even as analysts say voter fraud is rare and that there's no evidence of any systemic or significant problem. The Trump administration has pursued criminal charges in scattered cases across the nation — including in New Jersey, where officials recently found that 6,600 undocumented people had mistakenly been allowed to register to vote between June 2023 and June 2024, when the error was corrected. "Less than 400" of those people voted in any election, New Jersey officials said. U.S. House Republicans have launched an investigation. Meanwhile, Trump's executive branch offices have told state election officials they're criminally liable for registering or allowing a noncitizen to vote. ICE also has been trying to obtain voter data to investigate cases. "We think we have better candidates, and therefore, if the rule of law is followed, we'll win," an RNC official said. "We just are there to make sure that you know officials are following what the laws are." Zoom in: The GOP's legal effort is often opposed by Democratic Party committees and aligned law firms such as Marc Elias' Elias Law Group. One RNC official described being "ambushed" by the amount of litigation Elias' firm filed in a past election cycle.…

Why it matters: Washington and industry's failure to put basic guardrails around AI came into plain sight this week, spurring fresh momentum for regulatory action. Lawmakers were quick to re-up their AI bills following a stark warning that went viral from a former Anthropic researcher who said he quit the company over safety concerns. The post thrust the topic into public consciousness with more than 150 million views and fueled debate, but congressional leadership and President Trump have largely been quiet. Those are the players to watch for a true change in the U.S. AI policy approach. What we're watching: The White House and Congress have different cards to play. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said at the GOP convention this week that he wants to bring AI companies together to reach "consensus" on safety guardrails, "maybe even at the beginning of the winter," according to remarks his office pointed Axios to. A pause on the development of advanced AI, championed by the likes of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and likely to come up in a bipartisan briefing next week, would have limited effect without adversary buy-in, according to researchers who argue the U.S. has an obligation to stay ahead of China. Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping will meet at the end of this month, with AI safety on the agenda. The White House did not respond to requests for comment. On the Hill, there have been calls for new AI-focused committees, commitments from Democrats to hold hearings should they take back either chamber in the midterms, and plans to mark up existing bills. Between the lines: Without clear support from Senate or House Republican leaders — and by extension, Trump — Congress is poised to keep debating ad nauseam. The Trump administration's new framework for reviewing advanced AI models doesn't require companies to…

33e1d7779a:cc442bb3fa7895e4.title: Diesel hits $6 a gallon for the first time, fueling more inflation
33e1d7779a:cc442bb3fa7895e4.author: Ben Berkowitz
33e1d7779a:cc442bb3fa7895e4.summary: The national average price of a gallon of diesel jumped over $6 for the first time ever, AAA said on Friday. Why it matters: The fuel that runs the economy is getting more expensive by the day, costing businesses and consumers alike billions of dollars. While the $6 threshold is more psychological than anything else, it points to months of continued pain for drivers, shippers and shoppers. Data: AAA; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios Driving the news: At $6.0556 a gallon, diesel is about 14% more expensive than it was a month ago and over 60% more than a year ago. That is starting to show up in other prices, as has long been feared; inflation data out Thursday showed sharp spikes in transportation and warehousing costs, for example. Stunning stat: Brown University estimates higher diesel prices have cost U.S. consumers more than $46 billion since the war began. About 20% of that is in Texas and California alone. The intrigue: The White House's position is that fuel prices will come down after the midterms as the war with Iran winds down and oil supplies improve. But the Department of Energy sharply raised its 2027 diesel price forecast this week, acknowledging a painful higher-for-longer scenario. The bottom line: With diesel at $6, inflation looks like it's here to stay for a while. Ben Geman contributed reporting.

33e1d7779a:63f53d4a815290aa.title: 9/11 and "never forget" collide with the meme generation's dark humor
33e1d7779a:63f53d4a815290aa.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:63f53d4a815290aa.summary: America says "never forget" — but a growing share of Americans don't remember. Why it matters: More Americans are coming of age with no firsthand memory of 9/11 , creating emotional distance from the trauma and more room for dark humor and reinterpretation. The big picture: For Americans under 27, 9/11 arrived through textbooks, movies, social media and family stories rather than lived experience. That distance can make humor easier, amplified by algorithms that reward provocative content and a generational instinct to push back against mandatory reverence. By the numbers: About 83% of adults born before 2001 remember where they were or what they were doing when they heard about the attacks. But roughly 10% of U.S. adults were born after 2001 and have no firsthand memory of 9/11. That distance has allowed 9/11 to become fodder for a flood of memes, including ones using the iconic photo of President Bush learning about the attacks while visiting a school. Viral joke videos routinely rack up hundreds of thousands of likes, including clips with more than 900,000 and 680,000 views. The attacks have also become punchlines on podcasts , and in movies and TV shows . What they're saying: "I don't think I would personally sit and make 9/11 jokes," Harry Daniels, a 22-year-old TikTok star known for serenading celebrities, including President Biden, tells Axios. Daniels says it's difficult for some to "empathize or comprehend how massive 9/11 was if they weren't physically there to see it." "I think it's not cool to have empathy anymore," he says, adding that online culture rewards appearing "perpetually unbothered, perpetually unfazed." The other side: " I was at Hofstra [University], and I watched the building fall in real time," Jamie Cohen, a professor at CUNY Queens College, tells Axios. "It definitely f--ked me up... So now when I'm in a group chat where 9/11 memes come through, it's weird to separate the humor of the meme from the event." Cohen doesn't think younger…

33e1d7779a:3fcb61a9983efffb.title: Congress gripped by AI panic after doomsday warnings
33e1d7779a:3fcb61a9983efffb.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:3fcb61a9983efffb.summary: Anthropic insiders' warnings this week that AI could end humanity in the next decade have members of Congress frantically seeking answers and trying to cobble together some kind of response. Why it matters: Federal lawmakers are at the "concepts of a plan" stage at this point, with congressional leaders showing little apparent urgency to mobilize. Some rank-and-file members in both parties say something must be done: "We should absolutely act, and act with urgency," Rep. Johnny Olszewski (D-Md.) told Axios. Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) wrote Wednesday in a post on X that "Congress needs to convene a special session on AI and what the future of the U.S. looks like." Driving the news: Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon kicked off the frenzy Tuesday with a post on X declaring that "the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." Coxon quit his job at the AI giant after just four months to publicly raise the alarm about the dangers of the technology, giving up his equity in the process, Axios' Madison Mills reported. His warning was echoed by several current Anthropic employees, with one, Evan Hubinger, responding on X that "we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!" "AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction," wrote another, Samuel Marks. "This could happen in the next few years." State of play: Dozens of members of Congress — mostly Democrats, but a handful of Republicans as well — have since called for urgent action and floated a wide variety of legislative responses. Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.), one of House Democrats' most vocal advocates for AI regulations, is pushing his bipartisan bill to require AI developers to build a human-activated "kill switch" as part of any AI system. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said he and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) "will soon be introducing legislation ... to pause advanced AI and ban superintelligence altogether." Others called for a more…

Why it matters: The 42-year-old Vance, the first millennial VP, capped off the GOP's two-day convention here with a direct appeal to families with young children that emphasized the "birthright" of U.S. citizens. Vance also sought to cast Democrats as anti-American, anti-family "crazies." "America belongs to those who love it. Not those who hate it," he said. Zoom in: Support for Republicans is slipping across all age brackets, but the disapproval among millennials and young men is an acute concern for Trump's political operation because they were crucial to his 2024 victory. Millennials, born between 1981 and 1996, are the largest generation in America. They're also the cohort with the largest number of school-age kids — and particularly feel the bite of higher food and gas prices, driving forces behind Trump's low poll numbers. In his 41-minute speech , Vance established his millennial bona fides by mentioning that he's now the father of four young children who share in the "birthright ... to inherit the blessings of the greatest country on Earth." Vance's speech fell on the one-year anniversary of the assassination of his friend and ally, MAGA activist Charlie Kirk, who was 31 when he was shot during an appearance at a Utah college. "Charlie spoke to young men in particular," Vance said. "He understood that there was no greater calling for a young man ... than falling in love, starting a family and becoming a father." In contrast, Vance pointed to the now-deleted social media posts of a Michigan Democratic congressional candidate, William Lawrence, who once posted "fuck ... the nuclear family." Vance also attacked Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico and suggested he was too obsessed with transgender kids: "I never want to see that guy's web browser history." The vice…

33e1d7779a:2fcd712c94a913bd.title: Axios interview: The 9/11 photographers who ran toward the danger
33e1d7779a:2fcd712c94a913bd.author: Sarah Grillo
33e1d7779a:2fcd712c94a913bd.summary: "This is history, this is history." That's what photojournalist Spencer Platt was thinking 25 years ago as he photographed the events unfolding on the morning of 9/11. Why it matters: Platt and fellow Getty photographer Mario Tama told Axios what it was like on the ground that day. Trained as photojournalists, their instinct was to move toward the danger to document history. Tama had just been hired by Getty Images two months before when he got the urgent call from his assignment editor. Rushing out the door of his Lower East Side apartment, he recalled the horror of what he was documenting: "There was definitely some cognitive dissonance — it was totally unfathomable. As I got closer on foot, I came across an office worker being treated on the ground, stunned and bloodied. Seeing blood coming out of his ear made the human toll of what was happening frighteningly real." Tama credits the NYPD for saving his life that morning: "At this point, some other photographers and I began attempting to get to the base of the towers; as photojournalists, we are trained to get as close as possible. The NYPD likely saved a lot of lives that day, including my own, by blocking us from getting closer in that area." Attempting to access the towers, Tama witnessed the collapse of the South Tower. "I then heard a kind of sheering sound and looked up and, horrifyingly, I recall the tower tilted a bit and started to pancake down. In that moment, I went from being a photojournalist to any other New Yorker running for their life, it was absolutely terrifying." Tama took cover beside a parking garage with strangers as dust rained down in what he describes as a total blackout, holding onto each other in the darkness. After the dust started to clear, he captured a picture of the men he took refuge with: Civilians take cover as a dust cloud from the collapse of the World Trade Center envelops lower Manhattan, September 11, 2001. Photo: Mario Tama/Getty Images Meanwhile, Platt awoke in his…

33e1d7779a:ac5984147cdece0f.summary: President Trump acknowledged on Fox News Channel's " The Ingraham Angle " Thursday night that he plans to block Democrats' legislation if they retake the House and Senate after the midterms. Why it matters: Trump is already sketching out a divided-government strategy as Republicans fight to hold their congressional majorities in the. midterms. What he's saying: "I will end up being a blocker — I'll block all their bad stuff for two years," Trump told Fox News' Laura Ingraham. "It wont be the same. I'll be a blocker, what can I tell you? I'll probably be able to make deals with them. They are going to want some stuff. You make deals. It's one of those things." He said the current election isn't as "dire" as previous campaigns. The interview aired amid the GOP's two-night midterm convention in Dallas, where Vice President JD Vance and Trump were expected to speak. The big picture: Trump spent much of the convention's first night campaigning for the GOP and slamming Democrats, while also making promises to give Americans $5,000 checks. He also suggested in the Fox News interview that he didn't have any regrets about the Iran war, a contentious issue among voters ahead of the midterm elections. "I don't believe in the word regret," Trump told Ingraham. "You can always question yourself a little bit. And a few people have asked me that. If I had it to do again, I'd do exactly as I did."
